The complex kinetic model $\gamma_0$ was applied to simulate steady-state compression of a rarefied gas in a channel. The complex kinetic model $\

Voice assistants such as Alexa, Google Assistant, and Siri provide users with
easy access to a wealth of information through their mobile devices.
A key area of research in semantic parsing has been to utilize natural language
input from users to execute specific actions, like searching online or providing
real-time traffic updates. Most existing approaches to semantic parsing are
intraindomain, which means they rely on a fixed set of language patterns and
require a separate training process for each domain. This paper presents an
extensible semantic parsing system that allows for custom domains to be created
by specifying a schema that defines the required fields and data types for that
domain. The proposed system also features a language model that uses utterances
from existing domains to improve the accuracy of utterances in new domains.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine crucial information, precise measurements of heavy quarks produced in these interactions are crucial. To obtain this information, cutting-edge detectors are required, which will utilize advanced tracking and heavy flavor identification technologies combined with refined jet measurement methods. To obtain the necessary quark information, these detectors will need to operate at the same level of accuracy as present devices but also require novel heavy flavor identification methods and refined jet measurement techniques. This document discusses the state of the art in measuring hadrons containing heavy quarks and jets produced in interactions involving protons and light quarks, employing the most current LHC data along with existing measurements from the RHIC, Fermilab, and SLAC laboratories.

A new class of X-ray sources, known as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions, has been identified through observations made by the IXPE telescope. These sources, which are an accretion-powered variant of QPEs, exhibit distinct properties in their X-ray light curves. To study the variability of these sources, our team conducted an analysis on the X-ray emissions of four objects - NGC 4388, NGC 7792, MCG-6-33a, and MCG-6-33b. These observations, which were split into two sub-outlines, either covering X-ray flux changes, emissions, and color shifts, or emission rate fluctuations and spectral modifications during peaks and valleys in emission levels, were then subject to statistical assessment and spectral analysis. Our results indicate that the emissions associated with these sources' variability are largely due to Compton scattering of the soft X-ray emissions produced by a hot corona, which experiences significant absorption by the interstellar medium. These findings, along with the possibility that the emissions variability is driven by the same mechanism responsible for the eruptions, suggest a deeper understanding of the accretion processes at play in these sources.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long been known, but their intensity and distribution remain areas of ongoing research. Our study utilizes a three-dimensional radiative transfer code called STAG to examine the behavior of magnetic fields in a star's atmosphere, specifically focusing on how the temperature and opacity of the atmosphere affect the behavior of the magnetic field. Our results indicate that as one moves higher in the atmosphere, the magnetic field becomes weaker, which is consistent with earlier findings. Our study also shows that when the atmosphere is highly opaque, the magnetic field behaves more isotropically, whereas in low-opacity atmospheres, the magnetic field becomes increasingly aligned with the vertical axis, particularly when observed from an angle. Our findings suggest that when observing a magnetic field from a distance, its apparent strength and polarization may vary depending on the angle of observation.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds true in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using data from the MALTAS survey, we studied the dwarf galaxy NGC 4449, analyzing its H30α and Hα emissions. We found that the H30α data revealed previously unseen galaxies and helped us investigate the galaxy's central area. By comparing our galaxy's characteristics with other known galaxies, we discovered unique features of the galaxy system in the galaxy's core. We also found that using H30α is an effective method for measuring galaxy star formation rates due to its resistance to extinction. Our analysis of the galaxy's star formation rate and stellar mass surface density showed that the galaxy's star formation rate has declined over time and will continue to decline in the future. We found the galaxy's current star formation rate is lower than expected based on models of "bottom-up" self-regulation.

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate in case the group involved is $\mathbb{D}_{\infty}$.

We examine the approximability of the $L^2$-operator corresponding to a conditional expectation of a random variable influenced by another, as well as the approximability of the associated Markov semigroup on the $L^2$-space. To achieve this, we establish precise, testable conditions for the approximability in question, based on the properties of the given conditions' conditional expectations operators, which act on the quotient spaces of $L^2$ derived from an increasing sequence of sub-$\sigma$-algebras. We also investigate the relationships between the approximability of the conditioning operators and the approximability of the Markov semigroup, as well as the implications of these conditions on the approximability of the transition probabilities of the Markov process and linear operators related to Markovian transformations, within the context of compact operators.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models is complex due to the difficulties in determining suitable local and global observer gains. We propose a novel approach to calculate and optimize these gains by leveraging properties of epidemic model coefficients, which our analysis shows can be extended to transcendental functions. This innovative method enables accurate state estimation for continuous-time epidemic models with coefficients exhibiting nonlinearity.

Knowledge graph embedding is a technique that has gained significant attention in
computational science, particularly in its ability to model dynamic knowledge.
This work introduces a novel approach to incorporating temporal aspects of facts
into knowledge graph embedding. The proposed method utilizes a basic neural network
to learn and predict neural embeddings for entities and relations based on their
temporal scopes. By augmenting existing knowledge graph embedding models with this
approach, the duration of facts for entities and relations can be captured and
effectively integrated. The proposed method was successfully tested on two
datasets and CNGE, demonstrating its capability to learn embeddings within a
dynamic setting. Furthermore, the integration of the developed temporal scope
model significantly enhanced the performance of two popular knowledge graph
embedding models. Ultimately, the proposed model also led to substantial
improvements in downstream tasks, such as link prediction and multi-hop query
answering.

A new approach utilizing the Discrete Gaussian Beam method is presented to efficiently analyze the geometric properties of ring resonators, even in high-energy output scenarios with significant thermal effects. The thermal behavior is taken into account within the Discrete Gaussian Beam framework. Furthermore, the article documents the development of a computational tool for ring resonator design, incorporating both the Discrete Gaussian Beam and Lumerical tools.

While the development of federated learning has progressed rapidly, it still encounters a significant issue of heterogeneity that needs to be resolved. This issue encompasses heterogeneous data, model, client, communication, and deployment. A unified federated learning framework that can address all these challenges would be highly valuable, as it would enable researchers to create novel algorithms that can handle heterogeneous settings and improve the efficiency of federated learning. In this study, we introduce FLVer, a versatile framework for evaluating federated learning systems, incorporating its own API, heterogeneous data generators, heterogeneous model generators, optimization routines, and a monitoring dashboard. Through the integration of FLVer, researchers can streamline the process of designing, training, and testing federated learning algorithms by eliminating tedious manual coding, thus facilitating the exploration of next-generation federated learning solutions.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells, reducing their thickness below 100 nm is necessary. However, this reduction leads to a decrease in absorption, requiring the incorporation of a back reflector. Since metal back reflectors compromise cell efficiency, an alternative is proposed: using a photonic band gap crystal as a more effective back reflector. Since growth defects in photonic crystals are common, the influence of these defects on reflection properties was analyzed. By employing a transfer matrix method, the effect of various defects on the crystal's reflectivity was examined, and it was found that increased defects lead to decreased reflectivity. Specifically, it was observed that a defect causing a local increase in the thickness of the photonic crystal can significantly reduce its reflectivity. Furthermore, the potential benefits and drawbacks of using a photonic band gap crystal over a metal back reflector in terms of absorption were compared for thin-film silicon solar cells, and the conditions under which the photonic crystal outperforms the metal back reflector were identified.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu}$, defined in the right half plane, which with a slight shift effectively become iterated exponentials, $\exp^{\circ n}(\exp(z)+\mu)+\mu$, and remain bounded on the resulting antidiagonal set. These functions exhibit two unique properties, being their own asymptotic iterates for $\frac{1}{\beta}$ and possessing a family of fixed points. This discovery resolves a long-standing question that had been posed nearly thirty years ago in nearly thirty years.

We have developed a method to create 1-skeleton high dimensional expanders in the cohomology of classifying spaces using group cohomology and a variation of known constructions found in [Babai2009, Wu2009, Wu2011, Wu2011c, Wu2013, Lachish2020, Arora2020]. High dimensional expanders generalize expander graphs to simplicial complexes and our approach provides new examples of sparse high dimensional expanders. To support this we prove certain group cohomology computations and develop bound on the size of the first Z_p-torsion in cohomology and its relationship with the torsion of covering spaces.

Researchers have investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal GdInO$_3$ through a combination of techniques including neutron diffraction, specific heat, and impedance analysis. The results show that the crystal exhibits an orthorhombic monoclinc structure with spatial Pnma symmetry. The application of a direct current electric field can alter the crystal's morphology, shifting it to another structure that is triclinic in nature with space group P-1, due to the occurrence of phase transitions at temperatures of 100 K and 140 K that are associated with magnetic transitions. The application of alternating current at frequencies above 100 kHz can also induce phase transitions occurring near 120 K and 140 K near room temperature.

The application of graph embedding in various domains has been growing significantly, but a major challenge persists in handling large-scale networks with missing links. To address this issue, our proposed graph embedding method, Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE), focuses on sparse nodes and uses only their valid neighbor information in the network. In contrast to existing methods that require iterative optimization, SSNE avoids this by directly computing neighbor information without needing to iterate through intermediate steps. Our approach also eliminates intermediate steps altogether, making it efficient. To validate SSNE, we conducted experiments on real-world networks and found it to be effective both in terms of link prediction and scalability.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to create deep micro-etchings in 316 stainless steel for atomic vapor cells, reaching up to 2 mm in depth. The technique's simplicity allows it to replace traditional methods using deep-reactive-ion etching. Essential technical parameters are documented, including its speed and efficiency. The resulting vapor cells exhibit minimal distortion in flatness, enabling the creation of a functional vapor cell within a flat, engraved plate.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Timely wildfire detection is crucial for minimizing ecological damage, fatalities and injuries. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled real-time fire detection in video feeds. However, existing datasets for real-time fire detection are limited and lack diversity in terms of fire types and backgrounds. To address this issue, a new large-scale fire detection dataset has been developed. This dataset contains over 100K images and 70K video frames with fires, representing 11 distinct fire categories. This dataset aims to facilitate real-time fire detection in diverse environments.

Our analysis focuses on expanding the existing Twitter depression dataset by verifying
its accuracy and annotating entries with more nuance. We developed a novel metric
to assess the severity of depression in social media posts, categorizing them into
three levels: mild to moderate, somewhat severe, and severe levels of depression.
We also developed a filtering method to filter out posts such as spam, fake, duplicate,
noise, and those that do not align with the depression research context. After filtering,
we rigorously verified the entries' accuracy by having annotators confirm the original
annotators' work. As a result, the final annotated corpus comprises 10,990 tweets.
Notably, the corrected corpus shows a 15% increase in accuracy, particularly in posts
severely depressed. These findings serve as a foundation for future research in detecting
depression in social media.

This study utilizes Bayesian statistical methods to analyze time series data within the SIS framework. An machine learning technique aids in model selection among variants with different definitions. Predictive performance is evaluated and the outcomes displayed. Furthermore, simulations test the impact of implemented social distancing measures. Specifically, the use of lockdowns and successive waves of infections are examined and compared. Results obtained from our model indicate that removing lockdowns may accelerate SIS wave spread but could help reduce infected individuals' peak count. We also found that incorporating the incubation period into the model would improve predictive outcomes and the model's analysis aligns with observed data. This work aims to provide insights for policymakers to create future health management strategies.

Calculations of nuclear energy surfaces using a relativistic mean-field model with a specific set of parameters have been conducted. The model's parameters were adjusted to better match experimental data for incompressibility moduli of various nuclei, including those that are spherical, have moderate deformations, and are highly deformed. Notably, in the case of highly deformed nuclei, the isotropic second sound peak lies significantly lower than both the ground state and isotopic states, while in spherical and deformed nuclei with intermediate neutron numbers, the second sound peak is positioned between these two. This is in contrast to experimental findings, specifically a notable shift in a 20Ne nucleus that corresponds to a substantial change in its incompressibility modulus, from a lower to a higher range. This is better explained by a more accurate, higher compressibility value, similar to those in deformed nuclei rather than in spherical ones.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems with discontinuous Coulomb friction is conducted, and the existence of uniformly bounded asymptotically stable straight stick-stationarity solutions is proven, and it's demonstrated that the set of stable straight stick-stationarity conditions has a non-empty interior within the set of parameters governing the system's behavior, particularly, and the study particularly investigates the convergence of motion paths to either a curved stick-slip trajectory or a straight stick-stationarity solution under specified conditions, utilizing recent results on asymptotic convergence with friction.

We introduce a novel nonlinear problem in portfolio hedging that utilizes a combination of derivative instruments - options and futures/forwards, each offering distinct hedging benefits. This collaborative approach effectively mitigates tail risks through options while the remaining portfolio exposure is optimized to minimize variance when not in the extreme tails, with futures/forwards proving to be the most suitable tool for such purposes. The challenge is compounded by a limitation in the supply of liquid futures/forwards markets, making it crucial to identify the ideal set of assets that can be used in our proposed strategy. To address this issue, we develop a novel framework that determines the ideal portfolio of assets required to hedge a given portfolio. This framework is then applied to a given portfolio of assets to create a new, optimally hedged portfolio. We demonstrate the efficacy of our hedging strategy through a variety of practical applications involving real-world portfolios.

In today's commercial recommender systems, precise interaction predictions are crucial for maximizing user engagement. These systems typically utilize various techniques such as item popularity, user behavior, and personalization models. However, in this research, we examine how combining these different signals impacts the performance of recommender models. We introduce a new offline evaluation metric called Commercial Success that assesses the potential of a recommendation list to achieve its objectives. Based on this metric, we propose a framework called Online Commercial Recommender that dynamically selects the most appropriate model from a set of candidates. We conducted experiments on a real-world platform's data and found that OCRR outperformed its competitors in multiple scenarios.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out as a unique focus between the Fuchsian Heun equation and the Gausssian Confal Heun equation due to its regularity characteristics at infinity. We propose a set of formulas to transform a double confluent Heun equation with specified irregular singular points, characterized by the monodromy exponents, into a Fuchsian Heun equation, resulting in a Fuchsian equation with known exponents. To illustrate this, we convert a specific DCHE into the Fibonacci equation, ultimately enabling the Gausssian Confal Heun equation to yield a DCHE after an appropriate variable transformation. The resulting DCHE will yield a Fibonacci equation, facilitating the computation of relevant special functions via the Heine method. The outcomes will be verified both graphically and algebraically.

This work focuses on the underpinnings of a fundamental problem in low-rank matrix recovery where various blocks of a low-rank matrix are contaminated by Gaussian noise with heterogeneous variances, giving rise to a weighted minimization of the Frobenius norm in an optimization problem, specifically the weighted low-rank matrix minimization problem. We introduce a problem in adaptive statistics within low-rank matrix recovery that is analogous to the heterogeneous variance level in block-wise low-rank matrix minimization, highlighting the need to determine if this problem is non-trivial in certain cases. We demonstrate that block-wise low-rank matrix minimization is relevant to weighted least-squares problems in robust regression, also highlighted by block-wise observation and heterogeneous noise variance. We provide an in-depth, first-of-its-kind analysis of this weighted low-rank matrix minimization problem, offering both theoretical and practical insights that are crucial for low-rank matrix recovery applications. We start by identifying a key difficulty in this problem, the local minima of its loss function, and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for local optimality, as well as characterizing the set of local minima under certain assumptions. We then introduce the Weighted Alternating Least Squares (WALS) algorithm as a solution, with the key advantage of converging to the minimum of the loss function, given sufficient initial conditions, and analyze its performance in relation to minimax rates. We further demonstrate through simulations that traditional methods, like the minimum norm least-squares solution

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a finite, uniform, damped beam with one end fixed and the other end free. The presence of damping may unexpectedly lead to points in the frequency domain where different vibrational modes converge and become undifferentiable. These special points, known as exceptional points, can be mapped out for a specific amount of damping. Additionally, when considering a scenario in which both ends of the beam are restrained, another distinct type of exceptional point arises, exhibiting a complex and intricate structure. These unusual points in the frequency domain can be attributed to the underlying characteristics of a particular quadratic equation, derived using an analytical method, which aligns closely with the results of numerical simulations.

We introduce the composite biquark Lepton Flavour Universal EFT, named LB-EFT, to account for possible new physics effects beyond the Standard Model at the B-physics level. By combining heavy leptonically charged biquark states with the Standard EFT and LB-EFT frameworks, we describe B-physics effects that can be expanded in terms of inverse heavy lepton masses. LeB-EFT offers significant benefits, including the reduction of independent operators, enhanced symmetry, lepton universality, and a decreased number of new physics parameters. Furthermore, we outline LeB-EFT's capacity to be extended beyond tree level through quantum corrections, enabling calculation of corrections within the same framework. LeB-EFT's considerable predictive power and potential applications in future experiments are also discussed.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions and a central plant, all subject to external disturbances. By applying statistical inference methods to this framework, each agent calculates a feedback gain based on its current output covariance, estimated through an information-theoretic metric derived from its local data. This mechanism enables a decentralized and robust approach, unaffected by the influence of uncertainties and disturbances. We demonstrate the feasibility of this method by applying it to two representative agent configurations: a sequential setup and a network with interconnected agents.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction approach. The initial feature extraction utilizes a 3D-CNN model, while secondary features are obtained through classification layer output. The two feature sets are combined to enhance performance. The overall model achieves 84.48% accuracy, demonstrating superior performance compared to the single 3D-CNN model, which reached an accuracy of 71.25%.

Network science is a multidisciplinary field, leveraging mathematical and computational methods to analyze complex systems through their interconnected components. Over recent decades, advancements in network science have been particularly impactful in various fields, including biology, economics, and physics, where their applications to specific problems have led to significant insights and developments. Furthermore, these advancements often inform each other, fostering innovation and knowledge exchange. However, despite their importance, many researchers working in distinct fields may not be aware of these developments. This review aims to highlight the recent advancements made in machine learning over the past five years, focusing on both theoretical and application-based developments, and to illustrate how the community is evolving and responding to the integration of artificial intelligence into network science, as well as the emerging challenges and opportunities that lie ahead.

The interplay between evolving species and their surroundings has been extensively studied within the framework of eco-evolutionary dynamics.  However, existing models often neglect the significant environmental shifts driven by global warming, which typically have a greater impact on organisms than eco-evolutionary processes. To bridge this gap, we propose a comprehensive model that incorporates slow eco-evolutionary dynamics and fast global change influences. Our approach involves employing a singular perturbation technique to develop a reduced dynamic system and an alternative method using weakly nonlinear normal forms. We show that both methods yield comparable outcomes, thereby providing a more accurate representation of eco-evolutionary dynamics under the influence of rapid global change, particularly highlighting potential risks like extinction and chaotic behavior.

A significant challenge in automatic speech recognition and language understanding lies in acquiring large amounts of high-quality, expensive human-annotated data. To address this issue, recent research has focused on developing self-supervised learning methods that can train speech models without human labels, thereby significantly enhancing performance in downstream tasks. Nevertheless, scaling these speech models to very large sizes is hindered by computational limitations. This paper presents an innovative approach, combining self-supervised pre-training with a large 55-billion parameter speech model, utilizing the product of expert architecture to efficiently distribute computational load across multiple GPUs. The experiment demonstrates that this method successfully scales the model while maintaining competitive results compared to its single-expert version. Furthermore, it reveals that this technology can greatly reduce data requirements for fine-tuning on a language understanding task, thereby reducing the cost significantly.

Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based continuous auction system. 
We demonstrate the equivalence of AMMs to a specific type of financial contract, 
a 'log contract,' that locks in a static exchange rate. 
However, due to the highly volatile exchange rates in AMMs, providers often incur 
significant losses, a phenomenon known as impermanent loss. 
To address this, our study assesses the effectiveness of using decentralized stablecoins 
to fill orders in AMMs. 
Through simulation, we reveal that employing stablecoins can result in substantial cost savings, 
reducing losses associated with providing liquidity. 
Furthermore, the expected returns from using stablecoins can exceed those of 
traditional borrowing and lending platforms, such as Yearn and Aave.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on missing outcome data change under varying assumptions about that data. This concept originates from the principles of causality, particularly the counterfactual world. A proposed Bayesian framework for S-A utilizes prior distributions to capture varying assumptions about missing outcomes, with these priors based on a continuous scale to accommodate continuous outcomes. A CEF model is incorporated into these prior distributions to account for continuous outcomes. A hierarchical prior model is developed for regression coefficients to assess how these assumptions impact the model's posterior distribution. A separate prior is established for a probability parameter representing the missingness mechanism. Through these frameworks, the influence of these assumptions on key metrics such as the posterior mean, median, and 95% credible intervals for treatment effect parameters is assessed. Additionally, a sensitivity measure, referred to as the Sensitivity to Assumptions Parameter, is proposed to quantify the extent to which key metrics are influenced by assumptions regarding the missing outcome mechanism. Two case studies involving prior distributions for treatment effect parameters and varying probability parameters are presented to illustrate the applicability of S-A in practice.

We focus on $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the context of the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation, specifically its $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetric form. It has been established that the Cartan generator of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ preserves the equation's symmetry without changing the flow, effectively acting as a gauge transformation. However, the action of the Chevalley generator $E$ changes the flow, likened to a moving frame transformation. Furthermore, the paper investigates the integrability of the system, including its reduction to the $U_q(\mathfrak{sp}(2))$ symmetric DNLSE and related reduction and flow mechanisms.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence into Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has significant potential to enhance safety, traffic management, and privacy. However, concerns over the security and confidentiality of data in the traditional IoVs framework have hindered the adoption of AI. With the advent of Federated Learning, confident applications of AI in IoVs are becoming more feasible. This technology allows for the development of machine learning models directly from data at the edge, without compromising privacy. This research paper examines the suitability of Federated Learning for applications in the intelligent vehicle network, highlighting potential challenges and proposing innovative solutions. It also presents the utilization of FL for training machine learning models, along with applications of edge computing in the distribution and inference of these models. This research outlines future directions for FL research in the intelligent vehicle network.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has measured the production of $D_{s}^{*+}$ mesons in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, focusing on the forward region within the pseudorapidity range of 2.0 to 4.0. The production cross sections were determined and corrected for important influences such as parton saturation and the nuclear modification factor was calculated. The results were then compared to theoretical models and experimental data from the CT10 and NNNPDF3.0 sets of gluon distribution functions, revealing that the forward region measurements were sensitive to the behavior of gluons at large values of x.

The growing importance of cryogenic cooling in cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-systems for quantum computing drives the need for innovative cryo-systems. Our novel cryo-module offers an efficient solution, reducing size and weight while delivering a powerful heat removal capacity of up to 100 microwatts at extremely low temperatures between 20 and 250 millikelvin. The design of this cryo-module is based on a sophisticated two-stage cryogenic system utilizing high-performance heat switches and advanced cryo-module technology. The high-performance heat switches serve as an intermediary between the primary cryogenic stage and the secondary stage heat switch to deliver exceptional performance capabilities. Utilizing a high-efficiency cryo-module design with superconducting materials enables the secondary stage heat switch to interface with a state-of-the-art cryo-module grounded in a cutting-edge cryogenic technology. High-performance cryo-systems powered by a sophisticated cryo-module have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, achieving a remarkable 100 microwatts of cooling at 250 millikelvin. High-performance cryo-systems have shown the potential to support an array of next-generation applications including quantum computing, advanced sensing, and low-power cryo-electron microscopy.

Previous research, mainly focused on Node.js, has found that many Python projects use insecure cryptographic APIs, sometimes substituting them with weak alternatives, such as weak key generation in Python 2. Our research, however, analyzed the full range of Python APIs across various versions, reflecting the diverse nature of Python applications. Furthermore, our study encompassed the complete set of Python languages, including 2 and 3, and the extensive range of involved developers. Our results, based on a statistical sample of all Python projects on GitHub, reveal a concerning trend: nearly every Python project uses at least one insecure cryptographic API, with the highest risk seen in version 2 and 3.5 due to vulnerabilities like weak random number generation and API design. Notably, our study found a strong correlation between project popularity and security risks, with the most popular projects exhibiting the highest level of vulnerability.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed, well-known 3D objects in unstructured urban environments using generic 2D images. A complex urban environment simulation, incorporating realistic lighting, textures, and object localization, supports our method. A position-based urban object localization system leverages pre-computed navigation maps to guide a visual searcher,_accounting for sensing limitations,_ in an efficient manner. Additionally, our method inherently possesses robustness by utilizing generic 3D object models and maintaining awareness of object placement variability. A corresponding position-based learning algorithm adapts the system to unknown object positions. Experimental results verify the system's positioning accuracy and robustness while demonstrating its efficiency. Moreover, our method suits long-term operations due to its 3D object model updates, as well as its ability to adjust to changes in object localization through re-learning techniques.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within the context of seismic reflectivity inversion. A new formulation based on the sparsity of the reflectivity is developed. We utilize a novel sparse deconvolution algorithm that incorporates an adaptive, coordinate-wise optimization technique. Moreover, we derive a stochastic variant of this algorithm to enhance computational efficiency. Evaluations using synthetic data demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves superior performance compared to traditional l1-norm-based sparse deconvolution methods, ultimately leading to improved depth migration images through deconvolution-based inversion.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by Jia and Wu. Our study of BMOA-type spaces, particularly BMOA_2, led to a significant finding that semigroups of composition operators on this space are rare, in contrast to a previous conjecture by Berezansky and Vasilev about the existence of operator semigroups on Hilbert space-based spaces.

Understanding key properties like operator product expansion coefficients and conformal data is a fundamental goal in field theory, which can be analyzed at both perturbative and non-perturbative levels. Recently, non-unitary CFT data has been computed for 3D gauge theories using conformal bootstrap techniques. This research extends those findings to 2D USp(4) level-rank duality and calculates relevant OPE coefficients and conformal data in two distinct regimes. Notably, the research reveals a conformal vector field and provides closure of the STU algebra under the unitary representation for one of the CFTs, while another CFT shows dependence on rank-level coupling and contains multiple non-unitary representations.

As smart cities gain momentum, they necessitate a community of practice with its own operating principles and methods, which can be encapsulated in a context-specific domain ontology like CitySpec. This ontology can be employed to develop an intelligent assistant system such as CitySpec-Assist, allowing a user like Alice to interact with a virtual assistant that can respond to queries like suggesting nearby restaurants based on a specified budget and providing Alice's contact information to the requested service providers. This intelligent assistant not only aids Alice by automating routine tasks but also enables her to concentrate on her core objective of enjoying a dining experience.

To enhance quantum computation, error mitigation is utilized to produce more reliable outcomes despite noisy quantum devices. Hidden inverse operators are employed in quantum circuits to counteract noisy components and thus improve reliability. In this study, we conduct an exact analysis of qubit channel inversion and utilize exact inversion methods for common quantum circuit gates to develop novel gate inversion strategies. To propagate inversion through complex quantum circuits, we introduce the concept of an inverse circuit gate, allowing us to compare a few inversion-based mitigation methods with standard methods, notably zero noise zero variance (ZNN) and retrofitting. Our results, obtained by applying mitigation techniques to real-world experiments on quantum hardware, show that our approaches are competitive with ZNN and retrofitted in reducing errors. Furthermore, we observe that incorporating input distribution information into the mitigation process, analogous to an inverse circuit, yields significant improvements, particularly for advanced tasks such as quantum chemistry simulations. These findings suggest a novel approach to error mitigation, leveraging input distribution information, which may be particularly effective in the near-term of quantum computing development.

In a regular category $\mathbb C$, the cocartesian images of the finite idempotent monomorphisms form a finite, cocomplete, closed class of monomorphisms, represented by suprema of certain coequalizers. When a class of monomorphisms, closed under composites and post-composition with arbitrary monomorphisms, involves only finitely closed cocartesian images, it necessitates that these closed cocartesian images consist exclusively of finite idempotent monomorphisms, forming a finite, cocomplete subcategory of the category of monomorphisms. Consequently, the class of suprema of finite families of cocartesian images, when closed under finite coproducts and finite colimits, serves as a foundational element for the construction of a lattice of monomorphisms, particularly when this class is also closed under finite coproducts and finite colimits.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model, we study the co-occurrence of extreme weather in wind speed and wave height across various locations in the North East Atlantic. Analyzing historical data from 1978 to 2018, we found that extreme weather events occur frequently in this region with a probability of around 1 in 10 years. Our research demonstrates that strong spatial correlations between weather stations exist even at a distance of 500 kilometers. Furthermore, we discovered a greater likelihood of simultaneous extreme weather events occurring in the southern part of the region compared to the north. Our findings were validated through multiple methods of goodness-of-fit testing.

Recently, Contrastive Visual-Language Pre-training models like CLIP have gained significant popularity due to their remarkable performance across various tasks. However, the task-specific performance of CLIP is hindered by its reliance on a general-purpose loss and a limited class of categories in most cases. We introduce a novel approach that leverages knowledge from an external classifier to enhance the performance of image classification. This method, known as Alignment with Supervised Knowledge Distillation, or ASKD, combines CLIP's global alignment strategy with supervised knowledge distillation to guide the classifier towards a more refined decision boundary. Our experiments on the ImageNet-1K CLIP shows that ASKD achieves top-1 classification accuracy of 83.2%, significantly surpassing CLIP's 66.2% and even outperforming the fine-tuned CLIP variant, which attains 81.6% accuracy. The simplicity and effectiveness of ASKD make it a valuable tool for adapting CLIP to a wide range of applications.

To enhance the efficiency of nonsymmetric systems of equations solution, which are integral to many applications in computational science, we expand the elliptic operator shifting framework. This involves modifying it for both black-red white cycle red cycle black type 1 smoothers and Gauss-Seidel smoothers. Our analysis uses model problems to compare the effectiveness of cycle black-red white red type 1 and Gauss-Seidel smoothers in conjunction with pre- and post-smoothing. Our numerical results confirm the validity of theoretical predictions, which are either supportive or consistent with prior literature.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered as equivariant spectra with the group of symmetries $G = Q_8$. The analysis is carried out in the context of the slice category for $G$-spectral categories, with the specific example of the 2-sphere considered as a $G$-spectrum, denoted as ${}_{G}S^0$.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific characteristic (p), we introduce certain dual local invariants. These invariants enable us to define the concept of a ring being F-injective. We establish that this concept aligns with specific necessary and sufficient conditions related to the ring's behavior with Frobenius powers and certain specific modules. Additionally, our work includes characterizations of a ring being F-injective in specific cases (such as a two-dimensional ring) or being a G-Frobenius split ring with specific split properties. Furthermore, our findings have specific applications in the study of singularities of algebraic surfaces.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics is a rapidly growing field. However, a significant challenge arises from the fact that data is typically stored in a proprietary DICOM format, incompatible with common data processing tools and software. To facilitate further research, we introduce a free and open-source library that enables the use of pydicom for accessing DICOM data and integrating it into machine learning pipelines. By utilizing this integrated library, researchers can easily work with various imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, and more, in addition to non-contrast enhanced images.

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and demonstrate that the corresponding charge is connected to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. The transformation of the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term into a specific form is equivalent to adding a counterterm to it, resulting in a charge that is proportional to the entropy of the black hole. This charge is also identified with a specific component of the Brown-York Hamiltonian. By applying the Brown-York formalism to a Euclidean manifold with a specific type of asymptotic behavior, we can obtain a charge that corresponds to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. This derivation reveals a deeper connection between the Hamiltonian approach and Euclidean methods, as well as between the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and the Euclidean counterterm method.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to impressive advancements in genomic analysis.  Despite the success of these methods, deep learning models often struggle to provide clear and interpretable results, making it difficult for domain experts to understand and trust the results.  To address this challenge, we propose an unsupervised method that uses a variational autoencoder to learn a consistent, fixed-size representation of variable-length DNA sequences.  This representation can be used in downstream tasks, such as transcription factor binding prediction, and the use of graph-structured variational autoencoders allows for the visualization of learned structures and the identification of significant motifs.  The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through quantitative and qualitative evaluations on a public dataset, and the results show that our method can accurately learn transcription factor binding sites and that the learned representations can be used in supervised tasks with improved performance.

The interplay between a material's bulk and surface properties significantly influences its metal-insulator transitions, a phenomenon observed in various 5d transition metal monoxides. Through first-principles calculations, we've examined the influence of different surface terminations on V$_2$O$_3$ films, which exhibit a metal-insulator transition due to external stimuli such as strain, temperature, and pressure. Our results demonstrate that both surfaces contribute to the metal-insulator transition, which is consistent with experimental findings on ultrathin V$_2$O$_3$ films. Notably, our study reveals that the V-rich surface plays a crucial role in the transition and that it can be complete even with the bulk not yet undergoing the transition.

A new, systematic method for linearizing Lie-Poisson systems around their equilibrium points is introduced. Building upon the Georgopoulos-Kostant-Souriau theorem, this approach exploits momentum maps to achieve linearization. For systems derived from Euclidean motion, we demonstrate that a dual momentum map plays a crucial role in finding the linearized system's general solution. Moreover, we utilize Lie-Poisson system's integrability to develop an integrating factor for its Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The method is first applied to the heavy top equation and then generalized to the motion of a rigid body in a self-gravitating fluid.

A peculiar detached eclipsing binary has been identified in the light curve of the microlensing event MW16191462, which occurred when MW16191462 crossed the magellanic cloud region. The binary was composed of a trans-Neptunian object similar in size to the ice giant planets Uranus and Neptune, and the analysis for the first time, using data from NASA's TESS satellite and ground-based observations, revealed a substantial difference in the mass ratio between these planets. Additionally, the event MW16191462 provided an accurate measurement of the distance between the Earth and the binary system, using data from astrometry and a parallax measurement.

To address a class of hyperbolic conservation law problems, a novel control method is proposed, leveraging the $L^2$-projection technique. The study of optimal control problems associated with hyperbolic systems, such as isentropic gas systems without true vacuum, can be effectively addressed by this approach. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through the solution of an optimal control problem involving a particular case of isentropic gas systems, where it achieves an $L^control$ norm efficiency of around 99.95% after a relatively small number of iterations. The method's robustness and efficiency are characterized by an $L^2$-norm efficiency of around 99.9% after a state vector representation that exhibits a relatively low degree of sparsity, and it is notably resilient to the final time of the system's evolution. The method's success is also validated through additional numerical experiments.

Evaluating credit risk for bank loans relies on predicting whether an applicant will repay their loan on time or default. This assessment is based on supplementary information provided by applicants. We contend that applicants may conceal or distort negative data, leading the bank to make a flawed credit risk evaluation. Therefore, maximizing the bank's utility necessitates discovering any hidden data. This requires a combination of approaches: (1) encouraging applicants to disclose hidden data, (2) inferring concealed data from visible data. We propose a novel, data-driven technique called Adversarial Learning for Bank Loan Credit Risk Assessment (ALBLCRA), comprising two adversarial agents - the bank and the applicant - interacting to optimize the bank's outcome. The bank employs two methods to uncover concealed data: (1) utilizing a game-theoretic approach to incentivize disclosure, (2) employing a probabilistic inference technique to infer hidden data. Our ALBLCRA approach surpasses current solutions in terms of evaluation metrics, requiring fewer assumptions and operating at a faster rate.

Utilizing techniques from previous work involving just a few variables, we examined specific cases of the chromatic symmetric function $P_{\mathcal{G}(Q)}(x_1, \dots, k)$ for two important combinatorial structures, Dyck paths and arrangements of non-attacking rooks, ultimately proving certain conjectures made by Huh and Nagel. Furthermore, we addressed an open question in that regard. In addition to these cases, we derived novel combinatorial formulas applicable to the general graph $G$, and showed the relevance of our findings in relation to Huh-Nagel's conjecture.

This paper presents Orientation Convolution Kernels as a cutting-edge technique for generating Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs). By stacking these kernels, our OCNs demonstrate superior performance across diverse image representation types. In contrast to traditional Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), our OCNs excel in handling rotated feature extractions without increasing computational overhead. By employing a single set of orientation-specific convolution kernels, OCNs seamlessly adapt to rotational changes in input data. Moreover, our analysis reveals that OCNs facilitate more stable and high-quality feature representations, as supported by visualizations of feature maps. By integrating OCNs into a bag-of-visual-words framework for patch-based matching, we achieve significantly enhanced performance in the VIGR2013 and VCVC2013 image retrieval tasks. Notably, our method achieves a top-1 ranking accuracy of 64.4% in VIGR2013 and 44.5% in VCVC2013, a remarkable 2.4% and 1.7% improvement, respectively, over the rankings achieved by a comparable DCNN. These results were validated through a competition submitted to the CVPR 2014 Visual Circles Challenge.

Using a novel approach based on local harmonic forms, we have redefined linear periods on the $n$-dimensional group $GL_{2n}$ and linked them to characters of the group. This is achieved through the use of Fourier transformations applied to Lie algebra representations. Moreover, we have discovered that specific regular local periods on $GL_{2n}$ can be expressed in terms of simpler linear periods on $GL_n$. This is facilitated by using the properties of test functions in the group $GSp_{2n}$. Consequently, we have provided an alternative proof that local Bessel periods on $GL_n$ are independent of its dimension when it comes to being non-zero under unramified conditions. This was initially established by Jacquet and Langlands for the case of $GL_2$. Our work also extends to super-cuspidal representations, where we have established that certain local periods are non-zero, building upon the findings of Ginzburg-Rothstein-Weyman. This involves exploring the connections between different types of representations associated with $GSp_{2n}$.

We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses like the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ mass for a heavy quark flavor, with the aim of understanding the corresponding ambiguity. This method employs a novel renormalization group equation for the pole mass that remains unaffected by the mass itself. By implementing this approach and conducting precise calculations up to four-loop order for the cases of quarks and leptons QCD and QED respectively, we derive the magnitude of the ambiguity in terms of a short-distance mass parameter. This method not only provides the size of the ambiguity at each order but also enables us to track how it evolves as we move through different scales using the corresponding renormalization group equation. Our technique is applicable to other problems involving renormalization scheme ambiguations, such as those related to heavy quark masses.

We present an algorithmic approach that confirms a conjecture by Morel and Tsarug. It
is shown that if a graph's edges can be colored with a limited number of colors such that
each vertex has one color missing, then each vertex can be colored with a limited number of
colors in a specific sequencing pattern, with some sequences allowed for each vertex. The
algorithmic proof of this conjecture builds upon a concept called $R$-sequential $t$-coloring,
where each vertex has different sequences of missing colors based on its edge color
patterns, and has applications in identifying Hamiltonian cycles in graphs. This
R-sequential t-coloring is a variation of the k-Zarankiewicz problem and generalizes a concept
introduced by Alon and Tarsi.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and a parameter λ. This outcome builds on an enhanced version of the contraction formula initially introduced by J. Horowitz.

This study evaluates the capability of analyzing low-dose and ultra-low-dose
CT scans for identifying COVID-19, which offer a rapid diagnosis without
exposing patients to excessive radiation compared to standard dose scans. The
research utilized 100 individual scans obtained from 50 patients diagnosed
with COVID-19 and 50 with pneumonia, along with corresponding clinical data.
The scans were processed using a convolutional neural network to produce an
image classification output indicating the presence of COVID-19, pneumonia, or
normal lung conditions. Additionally, a convolutional neural network was
trained to detect the ventilation defect characteristic of pneumonia, utilizing
extracted features from the pre-processing network. The results demonstrated
that low-dose scans achieved an accuracy of 88% and a detection accuracy of
80%, significantly surpassing the performance of ultra-low-dose scans, which
attained accuracies of 70% and 50% respectively.

As numerous satellite constellations are being planned in low-Earth orbit,
operating under the concept of space occupancy to manage their mega-constellations,
a crucial challenge arises in predicting the likelihood of space occupancy for satellites
in polar orbits affected by atmospheric drag. Existing methods primarily rely on a
basic approach to model this distribution, however, this simplification becomes
insufficient under the influence of atmospheric drag, particularly in high-altitude
orbits. This work develops a novel method to precisely calculate the probability
distribution function of the height of satellites in low-Earth orbit, taking into
account the complexities introduced by atmospheric drag and the zonal harmonics of
the Earth's gravitational field. Our findings indicate a significant discrepancy
between the two most common modeling approaches, highlighting a substantial gap
in understanding the behavior of satellites in low-Earth orbit.

To facilitate the development of a versatile finite element framework, we have developed and tested a stable and efficient numerical approach for working with unstructured quadrilateral meshes of any order. The proposed scheme builds on the anisotropic algebraic eigenvalue problem to create a more flexible and efficient version of the Laplace-Riesz operator. By incorporating unique elements, we allow for faster computations, which in turn enables the development of specialized boundary conditions using a compact iterative method. The stability and performance of the proposed method were confirmed through the implementation of a parallel version, which successfully achieved high scalability on modern computing platforms. The average computational time per element was reduced by two orders of magnitude, and our approach also allowed for faster generation of high-order meshes, resulting in significant savings in setup time.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association strength between variables, yet estimating its population value from incomplete data poses a significant challenge in various research fields, such as genetics and the social sciences. The FastCorr algorithm offers an efficient solution to the population correlation estimation problem for missing data, achieving a relative error of at most $\tilde{O}(\frac{\log n}{\epsilon^2})$ with high probability using a single scan of paired variables, requiring only $\log n$ data to be examined. Moreover, the FastCorr algorithm can leverage an existing efficient method used in partial correlation estimation, allowing it to replace more computationally intensive approaches. The proposed algorithm represents the first efficient method for estimating population correlation of missing data in terms of relative error, surpassing previous efforts. The FastCorr algorithm has a time complexity of $O(\log n)$ and can process non-i.i.d. missing data in both fully and partially observed settings.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined in a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, with $d\in\{2,3\}$.  The problem is considered for $t<0$ and we seek a solution that behaves asymptotically as a strong $L^2(\Omega)$ solution.  The initial data is in a scaled $L^p(\Omega)$ space for some $p\in[3,+\infty)$.  Theoretically, this corresponds to the self-similar blowup scenario of a strong $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ solution occurring within a finite time in a forward-time scenario.  The key finding demonstrates the existence of a unique global forward-time strong $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ solution, under specific conditions on the viscosity coefficient of the backward-time scenario.  The problem's well-posedness in the backward-time scenario is shown for a broader class of initial data than in the forward-time scenario, thanks to the absence of blowup within a finite time.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been shown to be particularly effective in providing clear explanations to users for recommended items. However, the human-centric aspect of post-hoc methods has been largely neglected, despite its significance in enhancing the user experience through trustworthy and transparent AI. Our study focuses on the evaluation of post-hoc methods' impact on recommended system attributes, specifically in addressing concerns around latency, user control, and adaptability to user feedback. Our analysis, which involves a novel human-centric evaluation of post-hoc methods, reveals a hierarchy of characteristics that can be used to guide the selection of suitable post-hoc methods for addressing specific user concerns. Our findings aim to shift the current evaluation focus from task performance to human-centric aspects, in order to promote human-centric AI in recommendation systems.

Quantum wells made of InAs, a material with ultra-high electron mobility, face a problem with the surface morphology affecting the electrons' mobility. A new material system using FeAl$_2$O$_4$/GaFeO$_2$ allows for the creation of quantum wells in the perovskite-ferromagnet GaFeO$_2$ and the comparison of electron states at two different interfaces - the bulk and the free surface. The electron mobility is significantly higher - a factor of 100 - further away from the bulk, indicating that the material's internal structure is not to blame for the loss in mobility caused by the surface. The discovery of the material's room-temperature ferromagnetism presents the possibility of developing spin-based electronics with prolonged spin lifetimes.

This study introduces the first comprehensive framework for robustly learning unknown model classes through local membership queries. The approach leverages local, instead of global, membership questionaries, allowing learning from data that may not be uniformly distributed as long as there's local density near the target function. The framework includes both proper and agnostic models, with the authors establishing robust learning guarantees in a query-computation budget context. The results demonstrate that local querying not only facilitates learning more diverse model classes but also enables efficient learning within polynomial time. To validate the approach, the researchers developed both general bounds and instance-specific algorithms, as well as applied the framework to successfully robustly learn complex shapes and Gaussian-shaped hyperspheres.

Our previous research significantly accelerated the construction of a key matrix U using a Kd-tree, allowing for real-time performance. Building on this, we introduced the L/U-CoLT structure in 2021 as a Kd-tree-based adaptive task coarsening technique for reducing the complexity of the Schur complement in the geometric multigrid method. The Kd-tree structure of the resulting matrix L has enabled the design of linear time complexity operations for matrix multiplication, solving, and other operations. This presentation will detail our implementation of the L/U-CoLT structure in PETSc/TAO for an out-of-core nonlinear optimization process, and highlight our initial test results.

Young stars emit intense high energy radiation, potentially altering nearby planets' atmospheres and thus making them appear inactive. We investigate the effects of a young star's X-ray and UV radiation on an Earth-like planet's atmosphere, focusing on an Earth-like planet with 100% nitrogen, 2% oxygen, and water vapor, exposed to a young star's radiation. We discovered that a planet's atmospheric chemistry can be significantly influenced by its host star's X-ray and UV radiation, leading to atmospheric loss. We also found that a planet's atmospheric loss rate can be greatly increased in the presence of a young star's X-ray radiation, leading to atmospheric collapse. Our results suggest that a planet's atmospheric chemistry can be a reliable indicator of its host star's type and age.

We employ a theoretical framework, based on the quantum approach developed by Ginzburg and Frank, to investigate how mechanical resistance in a particle's environment impacts its energy loss through radiation. We examine the energy loss of high-speed particles in two distinct scenarios: when the particle moves slower than the speed of light, and when it exceeds the speed of light. Our analysis shows that the friction of the medium's mechanical properties causes an energy loss that grows in proportion to the particle's momentum, and the energy carried away by emitted quanta decreases, and the number of quanta produced increases, and the quanta's energy decreases, and the quanta's energy decreases, and the quanta's energy decreases.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, where the majority class tends to dominate decision-making, we've developed an efficient approach for jointly optimizing network structure and decision boundary formulation. Our proposed algorithm, based on iterative decision boundary reformulation, not only achieves faster convergence but also outperforms traditional methods such as majority filtering and over-sampling techniques in both binary and multi-class classification scenarios. Our results, validated on various classification datasets, reveal improved accuracy, reduced convergence time, and better class distribution balance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the simplicity of the approach allows it to be seamlessly integrated into existing machine learning algorithms, such as Support Vector Machines, for effective application on imbalanced classification problems.

We present the "Luminous" catalog, a comprehensive "quasi-stellar object" (QSO) sample derived from "Large Synoptic Survey Telescope" (LSST) data release 1, covering 100 times the sky area with redshifts ranging from 0.05 to 5.5 and apparent magnitudes up to 20. We have performed a detailed catalog analysis, including the sub-second structure of emission-line fluxes, a high-quality photometric redshift assessment, and a novel comparison of flux ratios between different emission lines. The catalog is presented alongside three key scientific outcomes: (i) a QSO luminosity function (LQSO) with six redshift bins from z = 0.1 to 6 and fitted by a single power-law, with a separate, well-constrained quasar luminosity function (LQSO) for z > 3 and fitted with a "Seyfert" and a "Broad Line Region" model, (ii) a "Seyfert" and a "Broad Line Region" model, and (iii) a comprehensive "Seyfert" and a "Broad Line Region" model. We have also introduced a novel model that describes the sub-second structure of emission-line fluxes, and used it to provide insights into the black hole mass function and the average accretion rate.
