Mechanical screening is a phenomenon in which an insulating background counteracts changes in an applied force field generated by an impurity. This concept has been widely studied in electronic systems, but its application to mechanical noise has been largely overlooked. Our research reveals two distinct forms of screening - strong and weak - in amorphous solids resulting from mechanical strains generated by active noise. In active matter, interactions between constituents can be elastic, and fluctuations in position can be caused by changes in applied force. When considering interactions that decay exponentially with distance, our research indicates that strong screening occurs when constituents' interactions are coupled with changes in applied force, effectively canceling out the applied force. In contrast, weak screening occurs when interactions that are linearly coupled with applied force fail to fully cancel the force field, requiring modifications to the applied force. Strong screening is found in systems with exponential interactions beyond a certain length scale, known as the Debye length. In amorphous solids, our research predicts strong screening is observed at distances exceeding a specific scale related to the impurity's strength and stiffness. In contrast, weak screening is found in systems with long-range interactions and fractal structures, where our research predicts an intricate relationship between the screening length and the fractal dimension. Our research highlights strong screening as a general property of homogeneous amorphous solids, in contrast to the previously proposed anomalous strain behavior and suggests strong screening is a general property of disordered materials.

Silicene's unique dirac cones are destroyed when placed on metallic substrates, 
  so researchers have turned to hexagonal boron nitride to study its effects.
  In this study, we used ab-initio calculations to explore the impact of 
  hexagonal boron nitride on the dirac cones of silicene and found that while 
  it causes inhomogeneous broadening, it preserves the dirac cones in 
  silicene. Furthermore, our results show that the dirac cones can be shifted 
  using an electric field, and on a certain range of momentum, we discovered 
  that only one branch of the dirac cones is present on hexagonal boron nitride.
  This research shows the potential for using hexagonal boron nitride as a 
  substrate for studying and manipulating silicene's electronic properties.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses an enigma with multiple theories proposed to explain its characteristics. Data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope, observing Sgr A East for three years, has been analyzed to investigate power-law emission above 100 GeV and potential GeV-peaked spectra. An extensive study of Sgr A East found an estimated 10$^{6}$-year-old supernova, indicating a Type IIb/Ib/Ic event. Utilizing data from the Fermi LAT and NuSTAR telescope, the evolution of electron and proton populations within Sgr A East has been explored. Furthermore, the origin of the GeV radiation from Sgr A East is posited to stem from the diffusion of shock-accelerated electrons through the remnant's magnetic field.

The paper presents a novel class imbalance handling method, which integrates the SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) approach with k-nearest neighbors classification tasks. Its objective is to create balanced training datasets by leveraging the structural characteristics of the original data, thereby generating synthetic data that is consistent with the original dataset. Our proposed approach overcomes the SMOTE algorithm's limitations by resolving the creation of a balanced training dataset. Our system involves a series of steps: (1) generating synthetic data using the SMOTE algorithm, (2) oversampling the minority class data, (3) creating new synthetic data from the oversampled data, and (4) classifying the minority class data using the k-nearest neighbors algorithm. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through experiments conducted on 13 datasets from the UCI repository, where it has been shown to outperform the conventional SMOTE algorithm, achieving higher classification accuracy.

This study analyzed data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news outlets to investigate coverage of COVID-19 and its contextual connections to a national pandemic survey. The findings revealed that the intensity of local news reports on COVID-19 initially surpassed the country's COVID-19 mortality rate but gradually became aligned with it over the following months. The research discovered that local news reports on COVID-19 were largely unrelated to the demographic characteristics of their audiences and, similarly, were not connected to the death tolls in their areas. The coverage showed positive correlations with a demographic referred to as 'vitality,' as measured by foot traffic and postal service data, and state-level mortality rates. The researchers found COVID-19 stories to be frequently accompanied by content about the U.S. political division over the issue, which showed little intensity variation across local demographics. The coverage rarely included positive stories about vaccination or high COVID-19 vaccination rates within the communities. The decrease in local news reports on COVID-19 was linked to increased coverage in national surveys about a broader range of topics, suggesting COVID-19 was gradually being integrated into broader local news discussions. The researchers proposed that this interplay between local and state-level coverage of COVID-19 may have implications for the dissemination of misinformation about the issue.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) is expected to naturally uphold the conservation of mass, energy, and momentum, yet previous studies found it falls short in doing so under certain conditions. This paper demonstrates that the conservation laws can indeed be satisfied within the framework of SPH theory, provided the right conditions are met. It shows that the total energy, mass, and momentum of a system are consistently preserved when using an arbitrary time step, as long as the system evolves according to the SPH framework. This finding resolves the controversy surrounding SPH's conservation laws and provides a solid foundation for understanding the conservation laws within this context.

Investigations into the structure of the proton have been carried out using elastic electron-proton scattering at Jefferson Lab, which has enabled a detailed examination of how energy transfer affects the proton's internal composition. The ratio of longitudinal to transverse proton form factors, G_E/G_M, and its impact on the longitudinal to transverse polarization ratio have both been precisely measured. The results of the ratio of proton's magnetic and electric form factors, G_M/G_E, were combined with the photoproduction cross-section to calculate a photoproduction cross-section ratio. The results of the photoproduction cross-section and ratio were then compared to predictions made by theoretical models generated by the Gen4 and GiGi programs, which describe the interactions of protons and neutrons.

We've developed data-efficient approaches for both reinforcement and imitation learning by employing a technique called synthetic state masking. Our method masks certain input states, forcing the learning algorithms to concentrate on the relevant, unmasked states. Through the principles of the Minimum Information Coefficient and Maximum Mutual Information, we ensured that the revised state representations maintain connections to the original states while filtering out unnecessary information. Our novel methods demonstrate a higher capability in extracting crucial states and surpass the performance of current state extraction techniques in reinforcement learning, while also exhibiting a higher ability in focusing on critical states during imitation learning. Notably, our methods demonstrate considerable data-efficiency in reinforcement learning and a higher resilience to noisy and disturbed observations in the task of block stacking.

A comprehensive search for the simultaneous production of two Higgs bosons at the LHC's CMS facility in 2018 is presented. These bosons decay into either pairs of b-quarks or pseudoscalar particles known as zero-mass scalars. Various methods to create two Higgs bosons simultaneously are considered, including mixed background scenarios. Due to a lack of evidence found in the data collected, no conclusions could be drawn for some scenarios. However, an observed upper limit of 0.14 times the Standard Model expectation was found for non-resonant production. Similarly, 0.29 times the Standard Model expectation was found for a Higgs boson created alongside a heavy pseudoscalar boson. These bosons would have masses greater than 600 GeV/c^2 for certain coupled self-interactions.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillation are capable of combining
high sensitivity with an extensive dynamic range, making them ideal for
measuring the weak magnetic fields produced by the human brain. We develop a
method that enhances the sensitivity of these magnetometers in its linear mode
by leveraging the ability to control the amplitude of the oscillation. Through
variations in the driving electric field, we can increase or decrease the
oscillation amplitude, which in turn allows for the efficient transfer of the
oscillating signal into the linear regime. Computational modeling using the
Maxwell-Bloch equations and experimental verification show that this technique
significantly improves magnetometer performance, specifically enabling a
decrease in magnetic field detection limits for weak fields.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. K3 surface automorphisms can be classified according to the type and count of Siegel disks they contain, and we will discuss the classification system in this context. K3 surface equations will be proposed for specific cases where K3 surfaces exhibit $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $5$, and $6$ Siegel disks.

In a supergravity unified framework, where the standard model is embedded in an $SU(5)\times U(1)_X$ group, we have proposed a two Higgs doublet model incorporating two singlet superfields under local $U(1)_X$ symmetry. This model breaks down $SU(5)$ to $SU(3)_C\times SU(2)_L\times SU(3)_L$ at the unification scale, generating additional neutralinos that contribute to dark matter. The neutralino's Higgsino component is a primary dark matter candidate, and its relic density is influenced by its interactions with baryons and leptons. These interactions are primarily mediated by $Z$ bosons and hypercharge gauge bosons, and we have analyzed the dark matter's relation to relic density, mass spectrum, and mixing angles. Our findings suggest that the dark matter's mixing angles are relatively significant, and the dark matter's mass lies within the TeV range. Additionally, this model addresses proton decay, Higgs boson mass, and matter-antimatter asymmetry issues, and we have explored the Higgs boson mass constraints.

The EPTAS approach initially developed for Maximum Independent Set in bipartite graphs has been enhanced for B-Matching, but it still involves a significant time complexity factor related to the size of the largest degree in a graph. In contrast, our research presents a new algorithm specifically designed for certain types of regular graphs - those where each vertex has a uniform number of connections. This new algorithm boasts a notably more efficient time complexity, eliminating the unfavorable factor related to the size of the largest degree in a graph, but instead incorporating the natural factor associated with uniform graphs - the number of connected connections per vertex. Our findings not only apply to B-Matching, but also extend to other related graph problems like Vertex Cover and Orientation.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks has been developed, dealing with a sum of convex functions that depend on individual inputs. Under certain conditions, it's proven that this algorithm is efficient in the non-asymptotic sense, even when inputs are discrete. The derivation of a key matrix approximation is unique to the proposed algorithm, allowing for a broader class of options and facilitating parallel computation.

Our approach to training a neural network for detecting hate speech in Hindi and Bengali involves leveraging transfer learning and data augmentation to address the challenges of low resources and unconventional vocabulary. We employ a BERT model pre-trained on language modeling tasks and further fine-tune it using the IM-Hate and DBQL datasets. To address the limited availability of labeled data in our target languages, we also apply data augmentation techniques. Our method yields strong performance on these datasets, with F1 scores ranging from 81.54% to 87.96%.

To enhance our comprehension of dark matter, astrophysics, and neutrino phenomena, we must develop more sensitive detectors. This necessitates integrating existing data from various experiments, as well as upcoming investigations, to establish fundamental limits that will drive future research. A novel approach has been established to consolidate recoil nuclear data from experiments with and without directional detection, as well as projective simulations, by translating them into a unified directional framework. This unified model can then be compared to theoretical recoil distributions, allowing for the extraction of optimization templates that will guide the optimization of experiments both above and below the detection threshold. This methodology has been successfully applied to interpret results from the XENON1T, XENON10, DAMIC, XENON100, and NAUTILUS experiments, demonstrating that existing recoil data have successfully ruled out isotropic dark matter candidates with macroscopic track lengths and certain neutrino backgrounds. Furthermore, these models can be utilized to optimize existing and future detectors for tracks, including potential upgrades to XENON, DAMIC, XENON200, XENONNATO, NAUTILUS, and others, to study isotropic and directional dark matter and neutrino scenarios.

A data-driven approach to predicting commercial vehicle driving behavior is introduced, accounting for the nuanced impact of contextual factors on this behavior. The proposed model leverages data from a substantial fleet of commercial drivers to generate behavior predictions, while a separate machine learning algorithm determines the most effective contextual elements for each driver. The incorporation of various contextual variables, derived from multiple sources such as GPS, weather, and calendar data, enables more precise behavior predictions. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through extensive testing on data from 20+ thousand vehicles, showcasing significant improvements in predictive accuracy compared to prior methods. Furthermore, this approach has practical implications for enhancing road safety and fleet management, as driving behavior predictions can inform behavior-based insurance policies and contribute to accident prevention.

This paper presents a new perspective on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) as a character detection task, requiring both locating and analyzing character details. Existing OCR models, however, face challenges in encountering novel scene text not seen during training, a problem exacerbated by current approaches' reliance on pre-trained detectors and heavy reliance on ground-level bounding boxes and transcription data. To address these issues, a novel character representation method and a novel learning strategy for character detection are proposed. A novel character representation method is developed to capture both texture and shape information, utilizing a novel text grounding task that enables rough character detection during training. Moreover, to enhance the model's generalization ability and mitigate the impact of overly precise annotations on performance, a novel learning strategy is proposed that utilizes character detection annotations with varied levels of detail. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these innovations, with the method achieving state-of-the-art performance and significant improvements on benchmark datasets. The associated code and pre-trained models are publicly available on GitHub.

Random fields, a fundamental tool in understanding spatial and spatio-temporal systems across various fields like remote sensing, geology, and biology, have seen significant advancements due to the integration of deep learning techniques. Building upon this knowledge, this study delves into deep learning methods tailored for random fields. Initially, it reviews the theoretical underpinnings and classical generative and discriminative machine learning approaches used in field modeling. Subsequently, it categorizes and analyzes the various types of deep learning methods applied to random field modeling, categorizing them based on the types of neural networks employed, such as autoregressive models, restricted Boltzmann machines, and generative adversarial networks. Furthermore, the study examines graph neural networks and recurrent neural networks in conjunction with long short-term memory networks and bidirectional long short-term memory networks. Lastly, the research delves into convolutional long short-term memory networks and U-nets, providing insights into the strengths, limitations, potential applications, and future research directions associated with each method.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(\mathbb{Z})$ with algebraic eigenvalues, we examine the behavior of the $L$-function $L(s,F\times F,\Sym^4)$ at critical values and show that its non-zero denominators, residing in $\mathbb{Q}(\rho_F)$ and raised to appropriate powers, remain bounded as middle variables' central values are fixed. Furthermore, for a Hecke eigenform $F$ on $Sp_4(\mathbb{Z})$ with algebraic eigenvalues, we investigate the behavior of the $L$-function $L(s,F^4)$ at $s=2$ and find that its non-zero denominators, residing in $\mathbb{Q}(F)$ and raised to a certain power, are bounded when the middle variable's central value is fixed. Building on this, we also establish analogous theorems for the automorphic $L$-functions corresponding to $\Sym^3(F_j)$ and $F_j^{\boxtimes 4}$ as a function of the level. Our approach to these thements involves adapting the methods of Bartel and Skinner to apply to the automorphic representations in question.

In a recent study, all-carbon graphene nanoribbons with hydrogen termination were studied using a computational approach that considers electron interactions more accurately than before. The researchers found that for nanoribbons with very large band gaps, energy differences between materials that have different electron spin orientations were significant and varied depending on the width of the nanoribbons. Interestingly, as interactions were considered more and more accurately, the initial prediction of a metallic state changed to a highly magnetized state with a very large band gap. Furthermore, the variation between materials that have different electron spin orientations and different energy levels increased dramatically, suggesting that this effect is a real property of these types of nanomaterials.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study extends the scope of existing results by addressing a broader class of operators than previously considered. To conclude, we illustrate the practical applicability of the findings with several examples of convergent operator sequences.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. The class of Hamiltonian graphs, which contain cycles of this type, can be identified through the following two conditions: first, if a graph G on n vertices (where n is greater than 21) has a connectivity of 2 and a common neighbor for every pair of non-connected vertices, then G is pancyclic. Second, if a graph G on n vertices (with n greater than 27) is 3-connected and contains a cycle of three vertices, then G is also pancyclic.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level has been studied and compared with theoretical models. The spatial imbalance of these collisions leads to different levels of asymmetry, which in turn affects the trajectory of light particles. The directed movement of light particles appears to be linked to the irregular spatial setup of these collisions, while also being influenced by the interaction between quarks and gluons in the early stages. The trajectory matches a model combining two separate quark and gluon fluids better than it does for other types of theoretical models. The difference in results might be due to the separate behaviour of quarks and gluons, while other models suggest that light particles are affected by both the quark and gluon components. The choice of theoretical model used to describe the trajectory affects how well it matches with the data, which might mean that the trajectory matches a model in which quarks and gluons behave differently.

The adaptive spectral tau method, initially developed for solving partial differential equations on square grids, has shown significant speed improvements. Building upon this concept, we introduce the sparse-grid-based ASK method for systems with multiple dimensions. This method utilizes a novel approximation to manage linear systems within sparse-grid-based time integration methods. Through rigorous testing on standard wave and Klein-Gordon equations, we verify the efficiency and speed advantages of the sparse-grid-based ASK method compared to traditional time integration methods.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a particular emphasis on solving the Schrödinger equation.  A significant portion of the review is dedicated to storing resonance parameters in a database, specifically the R-matrix parameters, which enable experimental data fitting.  Following this, various methods for extracting resonances from the experimental data will be presented in detail, such as the Wigner-Eitel method, the Fl\"ugge method, the Fl\"ugge-Beyer-Bruckner method and others that have been developed to address their limitations.  The review concludes with an examination of the merits and demerits of each method and suggests possible future research directions.

The Sinkhorn algorithm's convergence for solving the Schrödinger problem is revisited. A limitation of previous studies is that they rely on non-degenerate conditions, specifically that the given marginals must have full support, which is often too restrictive. We develop a theorem that ensures convergence of the Sinkhorn algorithm even when the marginals have degenerate scenarios, as long as their intersection is within a certain closed subspace of the space under consideration. This subspace's orthogonal complement needs to have a certain property for the theorem to hold, which is the case in many practical situations, including discrete and continuous cases.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 242 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV during 2017. The inclusive production of top quarks was measured when appearing as a top quark and an antitop quark, using events with one leptonic decays of the top quarks and 292 events with J/psi production in events with hadronic decays of the other top quark. The cross-section at a specific luminosity was recorded and compared with theoretical predictions, with no discrepancy found. Additionally, a separation of the individual cross-sections of the top quarks and antitop quarks was performed based on charge asymmetry, with results recorded and compared with theoretical predictions.

In a many-body localized bath, the dynamics of a central degree of freedom, such as an impurity, exhibit specific characteristics similar to those seen in equilibrium systems. The impurity's oscillation frequency, dependent on temperature, soon transitions into localized, temperature-dependent behavior due to interactions with the bath. Furthermore, when the impurity is coupled to a configuration with two localized excitations on either side, it demonstrates a localized motion pattern, unaffected by the overall asymmetry of the setup, mirroring the behavior of a central two-body localized system. Theoretical models and numerical simulations using two-dimensional numerical renormalization group method have confirmed these novel localization effects around central impurities.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ that guarantee the Bessel function $B_{p,c}^{A,B}(z)$ is $z/m$-subordinate to a function of the form $f(z)/m$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$ are determined under the assumption that $f$ is starlike of order $\sigma$ within the open unit disk $U$. Additionally, under suitable conditions on the parameters $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$, the parameters that make $B_{p,c}^{A,B}(z)$ close to star shaped within the open unit disk $U$ are identified.

Urban environments serve as hubs for economic growth and innovation due to their high occurrence of personal encounters and social exchanges. This study develops a technology that uses cameras to monitor and measure the number of urban interactions, its flexibility and scalability enable it to be deployed in diverse settings, such as streets, shops, and workspaces with minimal adjustments required. By comparing city centers to suburbs and tech hubs to financial districts, our data shows distinct differences in patterns of human interaction and demonstrates significant variation across years and periods influenced by external events like the COVID-19 pandemic. Analysis also reveals significant disparities between weekday and weekend interactions and distinct patterns on different days of the week. Our findings suggest a strong correlation between rates of human interaction and financial growth and innovation but also highlight the need to address data privacy concerns.

This research paper introduces and examines the development of a nonlinear field-split preconditioner, divided into two stages, to effectively resolve two-phase flow and transport issues. A corresponding two-time step solution method is also created and applied. Consequently, the proposed approach results in the linear system being significantly reduced in size compared to its single-step counterparts. Furthermore, the proposed two-stage, field-split approach exhibits a higher degree of robustness and convergence when applied to systems featuring distinct fluid properties. Comprehensive 2D and 3D two-phase flow and transport simulations were conducted using various vacuum-driven cases to validate the efficiency of the proposed two-stage, field-split approach with various field splits, demonstrating notable acceleration in convergence in comparison to its single-step counterparts.

The properties of chiral molecules interact uniquely with specific polarization of light.
A new theoretical framework based on electromagnetic theory and quantum electrodynamics
has been developed to study the interaction between light and matter at specific polarization.
This theory explains how enantiomers, which are mirror images of each other, interact differently
with chiral light in order to be distinguished accurately. It accurately predicts molecular responses
to chiral light in order to successfully identify the handedness of chiral molecules.
This theory also provides an in-depth explanation for the phenomenon of double rotation of polarized
light as it passes through a chiral medium, which is crucial for understanding the properties of such molecules.
The theory further helps in creating and optimizing systems for highly sensitive detection of chiral molecules,
which is essential for various applications in chemistry and biology.

This study explores the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti-de-Sitter spaces and two-dimensional string theory, with a shared two-dimensional open-closed duality. We find that the boundary contributions in their respective actions and string theory amplitudes exhibit significant relationships. We propose a "sandwich" representation for the sum of the boundary terms derived from closed-string amplitudes in two-dimensional string theory, effectively linking it to the path integral of Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity over a specific class of space-times, characterized by a given genus and topological twist. We then extend Jackiw-Teitelboim path integrals, including their boundary contributions, across various space-dimensions, comparing their characteristics with those of semi-classical string theory. We find that subtle boundary effects yield distinct results for different space-dimensions, with implications for the central charge in two-dimensional string theory and the cosmological constant in two-JJackiw-Teitelboim gravity.

A spacetime referred to as the Alcuberra warp drive metric is described by the Einstein Warping Equations, where a specific vector, the shift vector, plays a pivotal role in defining its unique properties. Due to its role in Einstein's equations, which involve second derivatives, finding suitable matter distributions capable of generating warp drive metric spacetimes becomes a complex challenge. Researchers have demonstrated the existence of anti-warping spacetime around a spaceship moving at subluminal speeds, but this problem becomes increasingly challenging as speed increases. The current research extends previous findings to accommodate any subluminal speed by employing a novel approach that utilizes a Fourier series expansion to derive an explicit distribution of matter surrounding a spaceship traveling at any given velocity less than the speed of light. The research identifies both regular and singular matter distributions capable of generating warp drive metric spacetimes, with distributions of both types considered in the research. The work demonstrates that singular matter is necessary for generating warp drive metric spacetimes, but it also reveals that alternative spacetimes, which are nearly identical to warp drive spacetimes, can be generated using non-singular matter, with both types of matter considered in the research. The use of both series of distribution of matter in the research provides an opportunity for future work to generate distributions of matter that have both regular and singular characteristics.

As urban digitalization progresses, the gap between established city services and emerging digital technologies widens, particularly concerning the management of underground infrastructure. Municipalities face the challenge of bridging this divide to efficiently manage and modernize their aging digital infrastructure. In this paper, we examine how three cities have developed digital strategies to address this issue and have been informed by a growing body of literature combining digitalization theory with public administration principles. Our investigation reveals a growing theoretical framework for city digitalization but highlights the need for further research in specific application domains to establish best practices.

To analyze a two-dimensional Wigner crystal's behavior, the spin of the ions is tracked over a long period. A theoretical model has been developed to predict how the spin undergoes dephasing. This prediction takes into account the crystal's charge fluctuations and external magnetic field, particularly its transverse component. The crystal's spin patterns and spin-related oscillations can be manipulated and observed, and this process can be repeated many times in a precise manner. This precise manipulation allows us to determine the crystal's properties, including its temperature and size, in each individual experiment. This method has the potential to measure the crystal's properties with high accuracy and could lead to the discovery of new spin-based phenomena.

TERS is an advanced technique that combines the capabilities of Raman spectroscopy with extremely high spatial resolution by utilizing metallic tips enhanced with optical properties. The technique is highly sensitive and can gather detailed molecular information at the nanoscale level, making it a valuable tool for researchers. Researchers have been able to enhance specific Raman signals using various methods such as tip-enhanced and surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, each providing different levels of specificity. Our study aimed to understand the individual contributions of these methods to RERS signals by comparing tip-enhanced and other enhanced Raman spectra. Our findings indicate that the TERS enhancement originates from both tip and substrate plasmon resonances, allowing for significant signal amplification – up to 10^4 times for specific Raman modes – which can help in distinguishing between different molecules. Our experiments demonstrated improved specificity in TERS signals, enabling clear differentiation between 5-ethynyluracil and thymidine molecules on a surface. Our research also suggests that the enhanced Raman intensity on a surface is influenced by the unique positioning of molecules in relation to the metallic tip, ultimately paving the way for more accurate chemical analysis in TERS applications.

Researchers have long studied Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME), a phenomenon attributed to the thermal motion of ultrafine dust grains at microwave frequencies. An AME-like emission was discovered in the Galactic Center region by Yoneda et al. in 2005, located southwest of Sagittarius A*. Our research aimed to examine the AmEmis data to determine the emission's source characteristics, distribution, and behavior. We found that some emission hotspots appeared in Sgr A East, suggesting the AME might be a non-thermal phenomenon, while radial distribution and time variability analyses revealed that most of the AME was likely of non-thermal origin. Our findings imply that some of the AME detected in Sgr A 2011 might actually be a new radio rebrightening of Sgr A East.

Ammonium sulfate, a common fertilizer and laboratory reagent, undergoes electronic spin transition and decomposes into diacid, exhibiting acid-base properties. Our comprehensive study, encompassing Raman spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and high-pressure diamond anvil cell, delves into the crystal structure and chemical bonds of this compound. Furthermore, our pressure-based investigation reveals the phase transitions of alpha-AmSO4, observing four distinct phase changes, and utilizes ITO coatings to enhance bond analysis through increased reflectivity. Ultimately, our pressure-range analysis, encompassing four phase transitions, validates our previous high-pressure spectroscopic findings, thereby significantly advancing our understanding of alpha-AmSO4's behavior.

In probabilistic learning, organisms are expected to adjust their choices to match the probability distribution of the rewards associated with the available options. This adaptive behavior can be understood as a balance between two potential strategies: one involves adapting choices to the reward probabilities, while the other focuses on selecting the option that historically yielded the highest reward. This study aims to clarify these strategies by applying two analytical methods - one calculates the likelihood of choosing the wrong option to maximize profit, while the other adapts choices to the reward probabilities of the available options. It finds that these two approaches yield similar results, supporting the idea that organisms may use a single strategy to accomplish both types of learning.

A novel interpretation of the Weyl chamber for the Lie algebra $E_8$, denoted as the root system $\Phi$, has been discovered using the concept of the Cohn-Denef--Sato vector partition function $Z_q(\Phi)$. This happens within the framework of the Dynkin diagram of the $E_8$ graph. Furthermore, by applying a vector-like quiversoft potential, we obtain an underlying mathematical structure of the Dynkin potential, thus yielding an alternative proof of a key identity originally proposed by Denef-Stafford-Staffel.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate nearest neighbor problem involves a dataset of polygonal curves and a query curve, to find the curves within an epsilon distance of the query curve, to within a certain approximation factor, taking into account the input curves' total length. Several techniques, including brute force, have been developed to address this problem with varying degrees of efficiency, taking into account input size, dimensionality, and approximation factors. A proposed solution leverages a data structure to approximate the total length of input curves, thus improving performance by an exponential factor in this variable, while still achieving efficient query times and a reasonable dependence on dimensionality and approximation factors.

To mitigate errors in near-term quantum computing devices, various measurement error mitigation techniques have been developed and employed. A novel method introduced in this research leverages Bayesian inference to account for discrepancies between actual quantum gates and their intended counterparts due to device imperfections. This approach is referred to as the Bayesian error mitigation method. A significant advantage of the technique is that it does not require gate-level control during device operation, but rather utilizes gate-level measurements taken from calibrated devices to inform mitigation. A key result demonstrates that this method consistently achieves optimal results, given sufficient data and noise-free conditions. Furthermore, the researchers showcase numerical results that demonstrate considerable improvement in performance when applying the technique, particularly in a simulated three-qubit device.

When humans operate robots or machinery, they often use familiar patterns of movement or actions, known as "motor schemas." These patterns can also be applied to assist robots in controlling more complex systems. To improve user experience, it is essential to adapt to and refine these motor schemas in real-time. Our novel system enables robots to learn and adapt to users' preferences for control methods through an iterative learning process. Our study involved 16 participants who operated a robot arm to complete tasks, and we found that our system resulted in higher task success rates and more consistent performance. Moreover, users reported increased satisfaction and comfort levels when working with robots that could adapt their learning methods.

This research paper describes the development of a novel mobile robot, named PEGASUS. PEGASUS features a unique design with six wheels to facilitate movement and is equipped with multiple sensors to gather data. The necessary software has been developed to enable PEGASUS to operate in unknown environments using local mapping and navigation techniques. Moreover, a virtual simulation of PEGASUS has been created using the ROS Gazebo package to test and optimize the robot's control parameters before physical deployment. Experimental comparisons demonstrate that the chosen software tools outperform alternatives in terms of efficiency. A user-friendly simulation interface has also been implemented to enable control of PEGASUS via a Raspberry Pi device with a touchscreen. Ultimately, this paper showcases the PEGASUS robot successfully navigating a challenging, unfamiliar terrain.

Research into two-dimensional arrays of wireless communication has gained momentum due to potential applications in multi-beam antennas, compact base stations, and cellular networks. To effectively design these arrays, it is crucial to understand the relationships between various parameters, including beam direction, element spacing, and the wave's source distribution. This study investigates two specific problems: creating optimal arrays with identical beam patterns through unique source configurations and the design of superposed arrays that generate the same beam patterns using distinct element arrangements. By applying advanced mathematical methods, such as two-dimensional Discrete Fourier Transform and the cross-correlation theorem, the research develops these two problems and provides insights into their solutions, which can aid in the development of these communication technologies.

Computed Tomography (CT) is widely utilized in both industrial and biomedical fields due to its extensive accessibility and versatility. However, most CT systems use a broad spectrum of X-ray rays, resulting in altered attenuation coefficients for different X-ray energies. This spectral mixture distorts images by exaggerating or diminishing certain features, creating artificial image patterns known as beam hardening artefacts. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed various CT reconstruction techniques that employ mathematical models to compensate for changes in X-ray spectra, known as energy-estimation methods. However, these algorithms are challenged by inaccuracies in modeling, leading to potential errors. In contrast, energy-weighting algorithms replace weighted averaging of individual projections, potentially eliminating beam hardening effects altogether, but this technique poses its own difficulties, particularly determining projection weights and dealing with polyenergetic effects during reconstruction. A novel approach, referred to as energy-weighting, addresses these challenges by shifting the weighting process to the data domain and incorporating weights during the reconstruction process. This algorithm, based on an existing reconstruction strategy, requires calculating projection weights and adapting the process to accommodate polyenergetic effects and numerical inaccuracies, and during reconstruction, beam hardening is counteracted by adjusting weights and incorporating total exposure data. A comprehensive numerical study was conducted to compare beam hardening, artefacts, and reconstruction speed among various algorithms, and to demonstrate the potential of energy-weighting in reducing beam hardening effects and artefacts effectively.

We investigate how electron spin interacts with light in thin metallic films, focusing on both light's electric and magnetic components within the material. We examine spin-dependent reflection, considering a more accurate model that accounts for light propagation in the material and how it changes near the surface compared to outside the material. Contrary to what might be expected, our findings reveal that spin-dependent reflection is stronger at oblique angles than when light hits the surface straight on. Additionally, our study reveals that the light model based on local responses fails at certain angles due to divergent fields, implying the need for a nonlocal model. However, this issue does not arise in a simplified model, suggesting that the model, despite its local nature, may still be applicable.

In this research, we examine the user's ability to locate and utilize context-sensitive terms in a visually guided interactive retrieval process, comparing it to automated methods. Given that human interaction plays a crucial role in effectively employing context-bearing terms for complex queries, our study aims to create the first user-based query expansion technique in view-based retrieval and evaluate its efficiency. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that human query reformulation is most effective when viewed through a strategic decision-making framework.

Time series data often comes with multiple variables, allowing for comparisons, quantitative assessments, and statistical evaluations of relationships between them. To work efficiently with this data, we need to understand its characteristics, such as trends, seasonality, and inter-variable correlations. Our proposed method, Temporal Surface Analysis (TempuS), combines visual and statistical tools to explore and analyze multivariate time series data, offering specific features like multivariate scatter plots and inter-variable heatmaps. Through our evaluation, we demonstrate the efficiency of TempuS in identifying patterns, anomalies, and relationships in multivariate time series data, making it a user-friendly solution for data exploration.

To enhance healthcare, leveraging data from Electronic Health Records is crucial. By applying machine learning to structured EHR data, medical interventions can be compared, evaluated, and improved, ultimately leading to better patient care. Despite the potential for model training, data quality poses a significant challenge due to the need for data validation and cleaning prior to training. In this research, a novel system called HealthQL is introduced, designed to automatically identify and flag data quality issues in EHR data using a comprehensive data quality lexicon. This data quality lexicon encompasses over 1,000 rules for identifying various data quality problems across diverse data types. Compared to manual inspection, HealthQL can pinpoint more than 10 times as many data quality issues in EHR data. Additionally, HealthQL is being applied to over 200 real-world public datasets in multiple languages to ensure accurate data preparation for healthcare ML model training. The proposed data quality rules are available for reuse at https://github.com/instanodev/HealthQL.

Using a mean-field approach and considering the intricate physics of molecular polarization, we study the electrostatic properties of a planar electrolyte interface. By accounting for the quasi-one-dimensional system, we introduce a nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann equation that takes into account the interplay of the electrolyte and polarization effects. The derived equation features a novel, position-dependent polarization term and is valid for any electrode setup characterized by fixed surface potential or charge density. Through numerical solutions, we investigate how the electrolyte thickness and stored electric energy change with varying system parameters. The influence of polarization is analyzed in detail, and the developed equation provides insights into the behavior of electric potentials in systems with charged surfaces and electrolytes.

Automating the labor-intensive process of extracting requirements from diverse textual sources is a highly sought-after goal. Recent advancements in NLP and Deep Learning technologies have made significant progress towards this goal, with notable developments in requirements-specific tasks. Nevertheless, existing models lack generalizability due to several challenges. Firstly, they rely heavily on specific datasets, hindering the evaluation of their true potential in diverse settings. Secondly, they typically incorporate only text-based data, overlooking other crucial textual formats. To address these limitations, we propose a novel, open-source framework designed to accurately map specific requirements to their respective forms. This framework employs a novel design that integrates multiple text sources, including diagrams, usage scenarios, and natural language, along with a corresponding attention-based model that leverages visual information. Through a combination of synthetic data augmentation and the use of visual text, our framework excels at capturing required information and outperforms existing models by a substantial margin of 10% on average.

In this research, we explore the network coding technique, specifically the use of maximum diversity network coding (MDNC), for downlink communications in Rayleigh fading channels, taking into account power constraints and perfect channel information. Our focus is on determining the optimal power allocation that minimizes total transmit power while ensuring every user meets their target signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio and individual rate requirements when using MDNC. Due to the complexity of the problem, which is non-convex and difficult to formulate as a standard optimization problem, we instead explore a related convex optimization problem as a starting point and then leverage the results to derive an approximate solution for the original problem, revealing that our solution is optimal under full rank matrix conditions and closely matches performance in cases of rank deficiency. Our simulations indicate that while using MDNC incurs a slight energy cost, the benefits outweigh this cost, and our numerical results also reveal that the gap in performance between the original and related problems tends to diminish as the number of transmit antennas increases.

A magnetic impurity on a superconducting surface generates unique quantum energy levels near the Fermi level, known as Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states, which have an 'up-spin' and a 'down-spin' orientation. These energy levels exhibit hysteresis behavior, mimicking spin-polarized memory storage. Research has shown that adjusting variables such as magnetic impurity moment or external fields leads to interaction between YSR states near each other, which can cause quantum interactions resembling Qubits behavior. Our research focuses on observing the interaction between two nearby YSR states created by manually moving two vortex cores on a Pb surface using the Scanning Tunneling Microscope technique. We discovered evidence of Qubits behavior by measuring electronic correlations connected with YSR states created from core levels 25 nm apart through STM bias voltage variation and core relocation. This interaction is confirmed by analyzing second and fourth order electronic correlations in addition to first order correlations in electronic field-theoretical language.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has made the most precise measurement to date for the $K^+ \to \pi^+ \nu \bar{\nu}$ decay process. By analyzing the entire 2010-2019 dataset, the sensitivity to this decay has reached $3.09\times 10^{-11}$, and either no Standard Model signal has been detected, or, with the assumption that the short-lived component of $K^+$ decay is negligible, a $90\%$ confidence level upper limit of $1.52\times 10^{-10}$ for the branching ratio of this process is established, representing a $40\%$ improvement over the previous limit. Furthermore, this limit aligns with the expected Standard Model value, but it is currently lower than the Standard Model value itself, mainly due to the inclusion of direct CP violation in the former and a 30% uncertainty due to the unknown ratio of $K^+$ to $K^-$ short-lived components in the latter.

Techniques such as NICE-SLAM, which register distribution-to-distribution point clouds, have shown significant potential in scenarios with significant distortions or non-regular point patterns. However, current approaches are susceptible to errors in scenarios with motions that alter the distribution of points. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel feature-based method capable of handling such dynamic scenes, including large deformations and object removal/addition, for the first time. By leveraging geometric features and their associated descriptors, our technique achieves more accurate initial registration, which is then refined through process such as outlier removal, outlying feature suppression, and self-correcting evolution. Experimental evaluations through visualizations, quantitative assessments, and extensions, such as 3D reconstruction and object detection, showcase the effectiveness and versatility of our technique in a variety of applications.

Satellite images are widely used in multiple sectors, encompassing fields such as weather forecasting, ocean monitoring, vegetation tracking, and military operations, to name but a few. With the increasing affordability of these services, the volume of satellite imagery has surged dramatically. The sheer volume of this data makes it impractical for humans to process it manually. Consequently, there has been a significant rise in the use of automated analysis techniques based on machine learning and deep learning algorithms. Although these methods have been successful, they typically require substantial amounts of labeled data, which can be costly and time-consuming to obtain. Our study presents an innovative zero-shot learning approach that enables automated analysis of satellite images, circumventing the need for labeled data. Our technique employs a multi-modal framework, incorporating both visual and linguistic data, to classify the contents of satellite images. The images are processed using various feature extractors to obtain different representations, which are then combined to create a comprehensive understanding. Our results indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance when tested on the EarthS-1 dataset, a collection of satellite images covering multiple sectors such as military, earth sciences, and environmental studies.

Pulse-resolved, nonlinear X-ray absorption spectroscopy can reveal hidden information about light interactions, but its development has been hindered by simulation complexities. This work provides a theoretical framework for analyzing specific types of x-ray interactions, supported by numerical simulations that explain experimental observations. X-ray absorption changes dependent on intensity are explained through ionization and x-ray scattering. These findings enable future analysis of x-ray transient spectroscopy, facilitating the interpretation of complex x-ray signals.

Recent studies have shown the potential of Deep Neural Networks (DNN) in automatic modulation classification (AMC) due to their capacity to learn complex, non-linear relationships between input data and desired outputs. Nonetheless, AMC remains challenging, particularly in scenarios where signals are heavily impaired by noise. Traditional solutions often involve designing features based on prior knowledge, but the effectiveness of such approaches depends on this information. In contrast, recent advances in deep learning have enabled DNNs to automatically generate features along with their weights, leading to more robust solutions. Moreover, these SOTA methods demonstrate better generalization capabilities. This study provides an overview of the most recent and promising SOTA AMC techniques based on deep neural networks.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions in MRI images is an unsolved challenge for deep learning approaches. Current methodologies rely on learning the characteristics of lesions from large, annotated MRI datasets. However, the limited availability of such datasets and the high cost and time required for annotation significantly hinder the development of effective deep learning models. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach called Active Learning with Uncertainty Estimation (ALEUE) that selects the most informative MRI slices for annotation. This approach incorporates a U-Net network to detect lesions and a Monte-Carlo Dropout mechanism to calculate uncertainty. By focusing on the selection of semi-supervised slices, our ALEUE framework substantially reduces the number of MRI scans that require annotation. We have tested the performance of ALEUE using data from the Multiple Sclerosis Lesion Growth Challenge and the Comparison of Deep Learning Methods for the Detection of Lesion Growth tasks, achieving a substantial improvement of 10% over the baseline model.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is developed, 
and its relationship to optimal transport conditions, specifically the MTW condition, 
is established. This concept arises from researching how measures with singularities 
affect the properties of optimal transport maps, and it's found that certain types of points, 
where measures have zero density, cause issues with the smoothness of these maps. 
As an application, this new comparison concept can be used to predict when points on 
a manifold's boundary, where a measure has zero density, cause issues with the 
smoothness of optimal transport maps, and also relates to previous findings about how 
density determines the smoothness of optimal transport maps in a special case.

This study addresses the trade-off between model complexity and a system's ability to generalize data in continuous-time systems, specifically focusing on identifying parameters for input-affine systems. Building on the principle of minimizing descriptive complexity, we derived a system's upper bound on its generalization error. Our analysis reveals that as the length of time intervals increases, the system's generalization error decreases, and the optimal system's rate of this decrease is (1/√T log T). Furthermore, the results are applicable to input-dependent systems, and the derived bounds are empirically verified using data from input-dependent systems.

A recent study of the Cepheus A region in a nearby galaxy, M83, has found the area to be predominantly composed of dark, dense, and relatively low-mass stellar and starless cores. Contrasting with similar studies in our own galaxy, this investigation found cores with much lower masses, with an average of 100 solar masses, in contrast to approximately 300 solar masses for our own galaxy's dense cores. Moreover, the study found cores with much smaller sizes, with an average of 0.7 parsecs, and with mass distributions that were significantly narrower. This discovery suggests that in galaxies with lower metallicity, like M83, star formation may occur in much smaller, and possibly in lower numbers, units.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can be detected through the gravitational lensing of compact objects like stars and black holes. A new gravitational wave detector called LISA, designed to observe supermassive black holes on a scale of millions of solar masses, opens up the possibility of detecting primordial black holes by observing how they interact with smaller, million-solar-mass black holes. A specific scenario is explored where a primordial black hole orbits a massive black hole at a distance where it can be detected by LISA as it slowly merges with it.

We conducted extensive research using advanced molecular dynamics simulations to analyze the liquid crystalline properties of wedge-shaped molecules with uniform shapes. Our results show that these molecules exhibit nematic and smectic phases with oblique lattice structures when packing density is less than 0.5, while adding more molecules led to the appearance of oblique-symmetric smectic phases. By measuring the angles of the liquid crystal lattices, we discovered that they are directly linked to the angle of the molecular wedges, while an intermediate range of molecular head groups allows the lattice to adapt to the shape of the molecular tails.

Our goal in this study is to tackle the challenges of memory limitations and high adaptation costs when fine-tuning large pre-trained models, such as GPT-3. To this end, we develop the Paradigm of Parameter- Efficient Tuning (PET), which enables effective model adjustment with minimal additional parameters. Following the success of model efficient tuning through adaptation of low-rank decomposition techniques for task-specific adjustments of a model's parameters, we investigate its applications to transformer-based language models. Our proposed PET approach combines this method for modifying cross-attention while introducing Task Adapter Parameters for managing universal keys in cross-attention, thereby preventing key redundancy and memory issues. Our experiments on GPT-3 show that Parameter- Efficient Tuning achieves performance comparable to full model fine-tuning across various benchmarks, and it also demonstrates improved performance on zero-shot generalization tests and robustness against distribution shifts. Furthermore, we demonstrate PET's efficiency gains on resource-constrained devices, such as the Raspberry Pi 3.

This paper investigates a complex problem where two large collections of data items need to be compared after dynamically adding new elements. Researchers examine the ability of deep learning models, specifically stacked LSTM networks, to learn and apply set theory operations such as addition and comparison. Through extensive testing, the study finds that learned policies can accurately determine the equivalence of collections with high precision, even when dealing with a wide range of element types. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the ability of these models to generalize to a wide range of test cases by evaluating them across multiple independent datasets with distinct characteristics, thus confirming their reliability and adaptability in various real-world scenarios involving set comparisons.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory to fluids composed of polymers yields the NPT equation of state, which in turn enables the derivation of configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy, revealing that these thermodynamic properties are interconnected through the ideal gas terms. Furthermore, the theoretical framework can be extended to calculate the chemical potential and Gibbs free energy, the latter being essential for predicting phase equilibrium in systems containing multiple components. Utilizing our generalized lattice cluster theory, we investigate the phase equilibrium of polymer blends and solutions, and the theoretical framework is exemplified through simulations of a polydisperse polypropylene blend, a polypropylene/polyethylene system, and a binary solution of polypropylene and polyethylene, all of which exhibit predictable phase behavior.

Transformer models like BERT and GPT have been shown to struggle with understanding and processing negation, particularly when it comes to reasoning tasks. Our research investigates how transformer-based language models handle negation in relation to common sense reasoning and explores how the models' performance is affected by the length of the input text. We conducted a series of common sense reasoning tasks, including 2x2,  NOT-2x2, Ferret, and GRIAD, to assess the models' ability to interpret and process negation. We found that, in contrast to non-reasoning tasks, both BERT and GPT models significantly improved their performance on negation-containing sentences when input length was controlled. However, we also discovered that these models struggle with more complex forms of negation, such as that found in the NOT-2x2 dataset. We believe that this highlights the need for further investigation into how transformer-based language models interpret and process negation in reasoning tasks.

In neural machine translation, the probability of generating a target word is closely linked to its preceding context, which poses a significant challenge. To mitigate translation errors, insertions and deletions are often necessary, but existing models primarily rely on word-level information, which is insufficient to effectively handle this challenge. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel approach that utilizes sentence-level context to guide structural modifications. Specifically, our method involves generating target sentences and their syntactic structures sequentially and utilizing syntactic-level insertions and deletions. To facilitate this process, we introduce a syntax-based rewriting network that identifies required modifications based on source and intermediate sentences. Furthermore, to ensure the insertions and deletions maintain sentence equivalence, our model is trained to minimize the distance between the modified intermediate sentence and an unmodified reference sentence that is normalized to EQNFS. By training our model to minimize this distance, we achieve better results in comparison to state-of-the-art models on English-Chinese and English-French translation tasks.

This paper introduces a symplectic framework for studying curvature graphs, enabling the computation of their associated weight distributions. By employing Fock-Darboux coordinates on a locally defined framework, one can recover traditional curvature graph coefficients. Additionally, the paper establishes the cross-product connection between symplectic curvature graphs and combinatorial graphs, culminating in a formula for the weights of curvature graphs using Fatourian invariants of Zassenhaus filters.

We investigate the large N limit of vacuum entanglement entropy for a black hole in anti-de Sitter space with dynamic time cross terms in four dimensions, in addition to general odd dimensions. Three-dimensional analysis is done thoroughly and confirms an existing vacuum entropy violation bound, but shows that the violation amount depends on coordinates, thus making it non-universal. It is argued that this non-universal behavior is linked to one-loop vacuum fluctuations. In dimensions higher than two, an analogous non-universal violation in odd dimensions is demonstrated. Notably, after integrating out non-geodesic parts, the remaining entanglement entropy shows a universal large N behavior that varies inversely with N, an behavior reminiscent of two-dimensional cases in both unitary and bi-unitary field theories.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution to Asian options pricing by utilizing continuous-time Markov chains in their 2013 study. This study focused on geometric Asian options, employing exact finite-difference methods to derive closed-form solutions. Building upon their work, we introduced lower and upper price bounds for Asian Asian options using Markov monotonicity properties. These bounds facilitate the exact computation of Asian option prices through finite-difference methods. As the number of states increases, our method converges to exact Asian option prices, thus enabling the pricing of Asian options.

This letter reexamines the case for primordial classical oscillations as evidence supporting the inflationary model.  They are the anticipated result of a non-linear dynamics transition during the transition from super-inflation to de-Sitter space, characterized by the transition of the Hubble parameter's derivative from positive to negative.  We showcase three distinct scenarios where this intricate mechanism arises due to field's coupling with curvature or scalar fields inherent in proposed inflationary models.  Given that classical oscillations have been observed in simulations of axion monodromy inflation, we explore potential connections to the observation.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial due to their interpretability. Although deep neural networks can accurately classify images, they often fail to provide clear explanations for their decisions. This paper presents a new method called Attention Refinement to provide specific reasons why certain areas in images are chosen for decision-making. This method focuses on improving existing attention-based classification models. It does this by creating a feedback mechanism that helps improve the quality of rough attention selections, specifically by targeting and eliminating unnecessary information. As a result, it enhances the clarity of these models. We tested ARef on six different image datasets and found significant improvements in classification accuracy and clear explanation quality compared to existing models with rough attention abilities.

Developing a realistic theoretical framework for high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate materials necessitates an accurate simulation of realistic cuprate materials within the quantum Monte Carlo method. In our study, we present a simplified model that replicates the interactions and vibrations found in cuprate systems. By incorporating long-range electron-phonon interactions that can cause both electrons and phonons to scatter broadly, our model reveals a distinct difference between how electrons and phonons interact with each other. When focusing on local electron-phonon coupling, our simulations indicate that these systems can be classified as weakly interacting. However, our simulations also demonstrate that, at an extended range, even weak electron-phonon interactions can significantly contribute to electron-phonon coupling, resulting in considerable electron-phonon decoupling. In our research, we provide direct evidence that our quantum Monte Carlo model accurately simulates local electron susceptibility and phonon spectrum, replicating key characteristics observed in cuprate systems. By comparing our results with experimental data obtained from neutron scattering, we demonstrate the importance of including long-range electron-phonon interactions for an in-depth understanding of cuprate systems.

This research investigates the underlying causes of HIV awareness across South Africa, a nation experiencing a significant HIV prevalence rate. Through the application of Bayesian causal inference techniques, we analyze the relationship between various factors such as gender, education, and proximity to urban centers, among others, and their impact on HIV awareness. Our study makes two key contributions: Firstly, we utilize the Bayesian causal inference framework to identify the causal factors of female and male HIV awareness, a topic of substantial global importance. Secondly, we evaluate the efficacy of the Bayesian causal inference method by comparing the identified causes with the results from established literature and observed patterns. Our research reveals that the primary cause of female HIV awareness is educational attainment, while proximity to urban centers is found to be the primary driver for male HIV awareness. The study's results align with existing research, highlighting the value of Bayesian causal inference in addressing complex real-world problems.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of the A$_9$B$_9$Cn$_2$Laves system, the study reveals an intricate order parameter structure, particularly under the influence of a magnetic field along a 53$^o$ plane angle, an orientation that corresponds to a fourfold symmetry axis in the experiment's coordinate system. This results in an unexpected topological defect arrangement, where a second-order helix reorientation transition occurs in the literature-unfamiliar crystallographic plane (001)010. A detailed examination of the emergent topological skyrmion lattice, especially its characteristics such as the skyrmion size, and the order parameter's behavior, has been conducted and the findings suggest that the identified skyrmion lattice may be a new, previously unexplored phenomenon.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models have become a significant topic in statistical research over the past few decades due to their potential to capture complex economic dynamics through a small set of unobserved factors. Despite their advantages, existing models face computational limitations, particularly in terms of time complexity and memory requirements, hindering their application to large datasets. To address these challenges, a more efficient algorithm called EM-DCF is proposed in this research paper. By introducing a representation of the factor covariance using the exponential kernel and non-negative matrix, it becomes possible to significantly reduce the computational burden and scale linearly with both the number of time periods and time series in each simulation step. Moreover, the proposed algorithm leverages efficient storage of intermediate results to overcome memory constraints. A variety of time-series analysis techniques built upon this algorithm are demonstrated using synthetic and real-world data, highlighting its advantages in terms of speed and scalability.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others as particular instances. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the existence and other solution characteristics of the equilibrium problem based on the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality.

Inspired by uncertainty-aware deep learning research in predictive modeling, we've adapted key concepts from this field for time-series analysis. Our research demonstrates that models like predictive deep learning can distinguish between uncertainty arising from incomplete data and uncertainty resulting from randomness, which has significant implications for risk assessment and understanding underlying dynamics. To illustrate the value of this approach, we've applied it to a simple model of neural activity and found a quantitative connection between the uncertainty components and the model's internal structure. This finding underscores the potential of our method to gain new insights into complex systems.

The debate surrounding the accuracy of mean-field dynamo simulations is ongoing due to uncertainties about the calculation of turbulent transport coefficients which drive the mechanisms for the generation and loss of magnetic fields as well as the effects of differential rotation and magnetic forces on the coefficients. To resolve this uncertainty, the most recent numerical experiments for a spherical shell of the Earth's magnetic field are evaluated to assess the accuracy of these coefficients, especially those related to the generation and loss of magnetic fields through the mechanisms of the Hall effect and the stretch, twist and twist effects. The results indicate that the coefficients which describe the effects of the stretch, twist and twist are well predicted by linear theories but the coefficients which describe the effects of the twist and twist are significantly larger than predicted by linear theories and lead to the conclusion that the open magnetic field lines are more likely to be generated by the effects of the twist and twist.

Our study of the galaxy NGC4945 reveals the presence of 11 molecular gas outflows, detected through the CO(1-0) line at a high redshift. The estimated outflow velocity is 130-1800 km/s and mass range is 1.1-1.6x10^7 M(sun). The study's findings are based on the ALMA observations taken near the galaxy's nuclear region. The outflowing gas has an average size of 1-100 pc squared, reflecting the influence of the galaxy's AGN. The estimated outflow rate is 0.01-13 pc year(-1), reflecting 0.01-13 pc year(-1), reflecting 0.01-13 pc year(-1), reflecting 0.01-13 pc year(-1), reflecting 0.01-13 pc year(-1), reflecting 0.01-13 pc year(-1), reflecting 0.01-13 pc year(-

In magnetized plasmas, the resonant interaction between particles and waves through their wave-particle scattering leads to a fundamental process driving energy transfer, ultimately resulting in particle phase space modification. This phenomenon is essential for understanding particle heating, acceleration, and chemical reactions. However, accurately capturing this complexity in simulations of various regimes proves extremely challenging, posing a significant obstacle to achieving reliable predictions. This difficulty is compounded by issues of numerical stability, necessitating careful treatment of the numerical methods applied to the discrete kinetic equations. This work investigates and compares the performance of different numerical schemes, focusing on their stability characteristics and the accuracy with which they preserve key properties such as energy, momentum, and angular momentum. We examine and discuss the implications of these findings in relation to accurately capturing Landau damping and the correct asymptotic behavior of the plasma distribution function.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have had issues due to the need for derivative information in error correction terms and the use of difference approximations that didn't maintain stability. This research introduces new formulas to circumvent these problems, applying them to the complex SGLM(3;2;2)(3;2;2) to achieve third-order convergence without requiring difference approximations or derivative information. Variable order methods are developed by using the difference approximation for SGLM only when necessary and without needing to reestimate step sizes at each point, and by employing even stage order functions. These methods are implemented in the code VARGLM2.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), using the weak* topology on the dual space. This inequality's solutions can directly indicate the C0-semigroup's stability. This method is applied to two specific operator classes, under the assumption of strong continuous semigroups, to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for exponential stability. First, we analyze the class of first-order differential operators in Hilbert spaces. Next, we consider dissipative operators in UHF unitary C*-algebras.

This paper presents an in-depth examination of matter-dimmuonium interaction processes, specifically focusing on the behavior of dimuonium, a muon-antimuonium atom, and its relationship with matter. Researchers are exploring the potential of dimuonium interaction processes as a means of detecting new physics, particularly beyond the Standard Model. A comprehensive review of research on this topic is provided, along with discussions of proposed experiments involving the interaction of dimuonium with matter at the LHC, LHCb, and Muon g-2 experiments. Furthermore, this review outlines plans for future experiments that could investigate these processes at the CERN Proton Synchrotron, along with potential experiments at a muon collider and a muon g-2 facility.

Portfolio performance is typically assessed against a benchmark like the Standard & Poor 500 index. Our study proposes a novel graphical approach to compare portfolio returns with its benchmark using basic statistical measures, which will be illustrated through real-world examples incorporating the S&P 500.

The interstellar medium of a dwarf galaxy is characterized by its unique properties, including gas phases, dust particles, and chemical elements. This study focuses on a specific dwarf galaxy called NGC 4449, which is being used to test theories about the formation of the interstellar medium. By analyzing this system, the researchers aim to gain insights into the interstellar medium's behavior in similar galaxies. This paper examines the properties of the interstellar medium of NGC 4449 by comparing data from a recent study and finds that there are similarities and differences in various regions of the galaxy. The results suggest that the interstellar medium in the central region of NGC 4449 is similar to that of the Large Magellanic Cloud, while other areas of the galaxy may be more similar to the Large Magellanic Cloud or the Andromeda galaxy.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in strong coupling between fermions and a broad range of boson frequencies.
